A hot water tank is not simply full or empty. Hot water floats on top of cold water, and a well-designed tank keeps the two apart, with a thin mixing zone, the thermocline, between them. Hot water is drawn from the top while cold mains water flows in at the bottom, so the thermocline moves up as the tank is emptied. The simulator in this appendix follows this hour by hour for one day.

The tank is split into horizontal layers. A heat pump charges it through an external heat exchanger: the charging loop takes water from the bottom of the tank and returns it at mid-height, and there is no circulation loop. A thermostat starts the heat pump when the sensor falls below the setpoint, and it can only run in the hours you allow. The tab Tapping profiles shows the predefined days of hot water use, with their sources, and lets you import a profile made with DHWcalc.

Open the tank simulator in a new tab. It runs in your browser and needs no installation. 

Figure 1 shows it with the default inputs.



Figure 1:The tank simulator with the default inputs: a 200 L tank, a 3 kW heat pump allowed to run in all hours and the profile “Family of 4, morning and evening”. Open the simulator to change the inputs.

The simulator is a single HTML file, 

dhw-tank.html. Save it anywhere and double-click it to use it offline.

The same model in Python, with comments on every assumption, can be downloaded here: 

dhw_tank.py. Running it prints the daily heat of each profile and the results for the default inputs.

This appendix documents the 3D version of the room CFD model in 

Appendix B: Room CFD model. The physics, the turbulence models, the advection schemes and the comfort indices are the same, and are only summarised here. The 3D model adds the room width: the side walls are real walls, and an opening can be narrower than the room, for example a window 1.2 m wide in a 4 m wide office. The model is made for comparing cases and seeing the physics. It does not give design values.

The model exists in three versions that give the same results:

room_cfd_3d.py is the reference version in Python (NumPy and SciPy).

room​_cfd​_3d​_numba​.py is the same code with the time step compiled by Numba. It needs the numba package and runs about twice as fast.

room_cfd_3d_gpu.mjs is the same solver as WebGPU compute shaders, which runs as the app on the graphics card.

Open the 3D room CFD app in a new tab. It runs in the browser on the graphics card and needs a browser with WebGPU: Chrome or Edge on Windows, macOS or ChromeOS, Safari 26 or later, or Firefox 141 or later on Windows. 

Figure 1 shows it while a run is going.



Figure 1:The 3D room CFD app with a window 1.2 m wide, 0.9–2.1 m high, 16 °C supply air and 6 air changes per hour, on the coarse mesh a few seconds into a run. The heat source stands in the middle of the room.

A run simulates 30 minutes and averages the last 10. Before a run the section and the plan show the empty room with the window, the exhaust and the heat source. During a run they show the instantaneous field while the simulation runs and the time-averaged field when it finishes. Three sliders move the long section across the width, the plan up through the room and the cross section (parallel to the facade) back through the room; a dashed line in each view shows where the other two cut, and two checkboxes hide these lines and the occupied zone. The slider beside the colour bar draws one isoline on all three views, for example the 0.15 m/s air speed or the 20 % draught rate; each of the three views keeps its own value. The draught panel shows the key results with three charts of the air speed and the ISO 7730 draught rate: along x at ankle height in the long section, along y at ankle height in the cross section (both also with the ASHRAE 55 ankle draught), and from floor to ceiling where the two sections cross. The occupied zone (by default 0.6 m from all walls and 1.8 m high) can be resized, and a button draws the mesh on the three views. A convergence chart at the bottom, next to the exhaust temperature and the energy imbalance, shows the rates of change of velocity and temperature and the floor speed 1 m from the facade at the centre of the window.

The app is a single HTML file, 

room-cfd-3d.html, with the solver inlined. Save it anywhere and double-click it to use it offline.

The room is by default 5 m deep (x), 4 m wide (y) and 2.5 m high (z), with the facade at x = 0. In the app the depth, width and height can be changed; the mesh is then set by the cell size (20, 10 or 5 cm), and the exhaust stays 0.1–0.2 m below the ceiling. The supply opening sits in the facade or the back wall and can have any width; it is centred unless y0 and y1 are given. The app offers the same opening types as the 2D app (a window, a balcony door, a top hatch and a low slot, plus a window across the full width), and the opening can be slid along the facade. The exhaust is in the back wall or the ceiling. The heat gains are a box standing on the floor. In the app it is by default 0.6 m deep, 0.8 m wide and 1.2 m high in the middle of the room, and it can be moved and resized, or placed by clicking in the plan; the Python examples use a box 0.4 m deep and 1.2 m high across the full width at x = 2.3–2.7 m. With a height of 0 it becomes a heated patch of floor (FloorFlux), which heats the air through the floor surface, as a sun patch does. The power is sized as in the 2D model so that the well-mixed room temperature is the same in every case:\Phi = \rho \, c_p \, q_v \, (T_{room} - T_{supply})

Instead of the single heat source, a room can be furnished from a layout file, a plain text file with one box per line (see 

room​-layout​-office​.csv):type, x0, x1, y0, y1, z0, z1, power_W
furniture, 1.0, 1.8, 0.4, 1.8, 0.72, 0.72, 0   # desk (thin table top)
heat, 2.0, 2.4, 0.9, 1.3, 0, 1.2, 100          # person, seated
furniture, 4.4, 4.8, 0.0, 1.2, 0, 2.0, 0       # bookshelf (solid box)
floor, 0.2, 1.6, 0.8, 3.2, 0, 0, 300           # sun patch on the floor

The type is heat (a HeatBlock), floor (a FloorFlux; z is ignored) or furniture. Lines starting with # and the header are skipped. The same file is read by read_layout in Python and by the app, under Layout, which also has three examples: one heat source, a two-person office and a classroom. With a layout the heat gains are the sum of the powers in the file, and the well-mixed room temperature follows from them.

Furniture is solid and adiabatic. A box takes the cells whose centres lie inside it: the faces of those cells are closed, so no air or heat passes, and the cells stay at the start temperature (grey in the app). A box must therefore be at least one cell thick. Furniture with zero size along one axis is a thin plate, such as a table top or a partition. It sits on the grid plane nearest to it and closes the cell faces in that plane, so it blocks the flow without taking up cells. On both sides of a plate, and on the faces of a box, the velocity parallel to the surface has no slip, with the log-law wall shear when k-ε is used.

The equations are those of 

Appendix B: Room CFD model with the third velocity component: continuity, momentum with Boussinesq buoyancy along z, and the energy equation in conservative form, for \mathbf{u} = (u, v, w). The turbulence options are the same: standard k-ε with log-law wall functions on all six walls (default), Chen & Xu, or a constant eddy viscosity. In 3D the shear production of k contains all nine velocity gradients:P_k = \nu_t \left[ 2 \sum_i \left(\frac{\partial u_i}{\partial x_i}\right)^2 + \sum_{i<j} \left(\frac{\partial u_i}{\partial x_j} + \frac{\partial u_j}{\partial x_i}\right)^2 \right]

Grid and time stepping. As in 2D: a staggered (MAC) grid with u, v and w on the cell faces, the projection method with an explicit time step, and TVD (van Leer) or upwind advection. The default grid is 50 × 40 × 25 cells (10 cm), which is 50,000 cells against 5,000 in the 2D section.

Pressure. The pressure equation is the costly part in 3D. A direct solver, as used in 2D, does not scale: on 50,000 cells the LU factor has about 27 million entries. The 3D model therefore solves the pressure equation iteratively, with conjugate gradients preconditioned by one multigrid V-cycle 

Trottenberg et al., 2001. The cells are grouped 2 × 2 × 2 into coarser grids until fewer than a few hundred cells are left, the error is smoothed by weighted Jacobi sweeps on each grid, and the coarsest grid is solved directly. Each time step starts from the pressure of the previous step and stops when the residual has fallen by a factor 

106, which changes the temperatures by less than 

10-4 K compared with 

10-8. The number of iterations hardly grows with the number of cells, typically 3–10 per time step.

Numba. 

room​_cfd​_3d​_numba​.py turns each stage of the time step into one compiled loop over the cells, run in parallel on all processor cores. The pressure solve still takes about 80 % of the run time, so the gain is a factor of about 2 (see the run times below).

WebGPU. 

room_cfd_3d_gpu.mjs runs the whole time loop on the graphics card, including the time step and the dot products of the pressure solver, so data only comes back to the page for plotting. The differences from the Python version are:

Single precision, because WGSL has no double precision. Temperature is stored as the deviation from the start value to keep the small changes per time step.

The multigrid uses plain aggregation with 7-point coarse operators (half the Galerkin product), so every grid level is a simple stencil that runs well on a GPU, and an exact solve on the coarsest grid of at most 128 cells.

Validation against measurements. The IEA Annex 20 room 

Nielsen, 1990 was run in 3D with the slot across the full width (W = H = 3 m assumed) on 72 × 18 × 36 cells. The flow is not two-dimensional: the net flow through the line x = H is 0.13 of the supply flow at mid-width and up to 1.6 near the side walls, so the return flow is pushed to the sides. On this coarse grid the errors are 0.07–0.15 u_0 on three of the four measuring lines and 0.30 u_0 on the line under the ceiling, close to the 2D model on the same x-z grid (0.05–0.30 u_0). This appendix documents a small 2D computational fluid dynamics (CFD) model of a room section. It is used in Part D to show how the placement of an opening, the supply temperature and the airflow decide whether ventilative cooling gives draught at the feet. The model is made for comparing cases and seeing the physics. It does not give design values.

The model exists in two versions that give the same results:

room_cfd.py is the reference version in Python, with plotting functions in 

room_cfd_plots.py and the figures of this appendix in 

cfd_examples.py.

room-cfd.mjs is the same solver in JavaScript, which runs as the app.

Open the room CFD app in a new tab. It runs in your browser and needs no installation. 

Figure 1 shows it after a run with the default inputs.



Figure 1:The room CFD app after a run with the default inputs: a window from 0.9 to 2.1 m, 16 °C supply air and 6 air changes per hour. Open the app to change the inputs.

The app starts a run when it opens. A run simulates 30 minutes of real time and takes under a minute in a browser. The section view shows the instantaneous field while the simulation runs and the time-averaged field when it finishes. Changing a setting starts a new run.

Under Room you can change the depth of the room from the facade (3–10 m) and the ceiling height (2.4–4 m). A third slider moves the 0.4 m wide block of heat gains along the floor. The exhaust slot stays 0.1–0.2 m below the ceiling, and the cells keep the size set under Mesh. The slider beside the colour bar draws one isoline on the section, for example the 0.15 m/s air speed or the 20 % draught rate. Each of the three views keeps its own value.

The app is a single HTML file, 

room-cfd.html. Save it anywhere and double-click it to use it offline.

The model is a vertical section through a room 5 m deep and 2.5 m high. The room is 4 m wide, which is only used to turn the airflow and the heat gains into values per metre of width. The supply opening sits in the facade at x = 0 and the exhaust is a 0.1 m slot high in the back wall, at 2.3–2.4 m.

The heat gains (people, equipment and sun-heated surfaces lumped together) are a heat source in a block 0.4 m wide and 1.2 m high in the middle of the room. Their size is set so that the well-mixed room temperature is the same in every case:\Phi = \rho \, c_p \, q_v \, (T_{room} - T_{supply})

A colder supply then means more cooling, which is what a designer compares. If the gains were kept fixed instead, a colder supply would only lower the whole temperature field and the flow pattern would not change, because buoyancy depends on temperature differences and not on the temperature level.

The air is treated as incompressible, with buoyancy from the Boussinesq approximation: the density is constant except in the gravity term, where it varies with temperature through the thermal expansion coefficient  eta = 1/T_{ref} (ideal gas, T_{ref} in kelvin). Here 
u = 1.5 \cdot 10^{-5} m²/s is the molecular viscosity of air, 
u_t the eddy viscosity from the turbulence model, Pr_t = 0.85 the turbulent Prandtl number and S the heat source in W/m³. The temperature equation is in conservative (flux) form, so the energy balance of the room closes exactly.

The flow in a ventilated room is turbulent, and the model does not resolve the eddies. Instead it adds an eddy viscosity \nu_t that represents the mixing they cause. Three options are available.

k-ε (default). The standard two-equation model of 

Launder & Spalding (1974). Two extra transport equations carry the turbulent kinetic energy k and its dissipation rate \varepsilon through the room, and the eddy viscosity follows from them:\nu_t = C_\mu \frac{k^2}{\varepsilon}, \qquad
\frac{Dk}{Dt} = \nabla \cdot \left[ \left(\nu + \frac{\nu_t}{\sigma_k}\right) \nabla k \right] + P_k + G_b - \varepsilon, \qquad
\frac{D\varepsilon}{Dt} = \nabla \cdot \left[ \left(\nu + \frac{\nu_t}{\sigma_\varepsilon}\right) \nabla \varepsilon \right] + C_1 \frac{\varepsilon}{k} \left(P_k + G_b^+\right) - C_2 \frac{\varepsilon^2}{k}

P_k = \nu_t \left[ 2 (\partial u / \partial x)^2 + 2 (\partial v / \partial y)^2 + (\partial u / \partial y + \partial v / \partial x)^2 \right] is the production by shear and G_b = -g \beta (\nu_t / Pr_t) \, \partial T / \partial y the production by buoyancy, which is negative in a stable layer and damps the turbulence there. The constants are the standard ones: C_\mu = 0.09, C_1 = 1.44, C_2 = 1.92, \sigma_k = 1.0 and \sigma_\varepsilon = 1.3. The grid is too coarse to resolve the thin layer next to a wall, so the first cell uses wall functions: the wall shear stress follows the logarithmic law of the wall, and \varepsilon in that cell is set from the local equilibrium \varepsilon = C_\mu^{3/4} k^{3/2} / (\kappa \, y_p). The supply air carries k = 1.5 (Tu_{in} U)^2 with Tu_{in} = 4 % and \varepsilon = k^{3/2} / (0.1 \, h_{open}), as in the IEA Annex 20 test case 

Nielsen, 1990. This turbulence model is the only one of the three implemented models that passes that test (see Verification).

Chen & Xu. A zero-equation model developed for indoor air 

:\nu_t = 0.03874 \, V \, \ell

with V the local mean speed and \ell the distance to the nearest wall. It gives little mixing near walls and in still air, and more mixing in the jet.

Constant. One eddy viscosity everywhere, by default \nu_t = 0.002 m²/s, which is about 130 times the molecular value.

Chen & Xu and the constant viscosity models are implemented for comparison, because they show what a turbulence model do.

Grid. The section is divided into equal rectangular cells, 100 × 50 by default in Python (cells of 5 cm) and 60 × 30 in the app. The grid is staggered (a MAC grid, 

): the pressure and the temperature sit in the cell centres, u on the vertical cell faces and v on the horizontal faces. This arrangement couples pressure and velocity tightly and avoids the checkerboard pressure oscillations that a collocated grid suffers from.

Time stepping. The model marches in time with the projection method of 

. Each time step has three parts:

Advance the velocity without the pressure gradient, using the advection, diffusion and buoyancy terms. This gives an intermediate velocity \mathbf{u}^* that does not yet satisfy continuity.

Solve a Poisson equation for the pressure, \nabla^2 p = \rho \, \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}^* / \Delta t. The matrix depends only on the grid and the boundary types, so it is factorised once before the run (sparse LU in Python, banded Cholesky in JavaScript), and each step only needs a back-substitution.

Correct the velocity with the pressure gradient, \mathbf{u}^{n+1} = \mathbf{u}^* - \Delta t \, \nabla p / \rho. The corrected field satisfies continuity to machine precision.

The temperature, and with k-ε model also k and \varepsilon, are then advanced with the new velocity. The sink terms of k and \varepsilon are treated implicitly so that both stay positive, and k and \varepsilon use upwind advection. The time step is set at every step from the stability limits of the explicit scheme:\Delta t = \min \left( C \frac{\Delta x}{|u|_{max}}, \; 0.2 \frac{\Delta x^2}{\nu_{max}}, \; 0.5 \text{ s} \right)

with the Courant number C = 0.25 for the TVD scheme and 0.4 for upwind. With 5 cm cells and 0.4 m/s jets this gives time steps of about 0.03 s, so a 30-minute run takes about 50,000 steps.

Why march in time. A steady solver (like SIMPLE in commercial codes) would be faster when the flow has a steady state, but cold air from a window falling into a warm room often flaps and wanders and has none. A time-marching solver handles both cases: it settles if the flow is steady, and it averages if it is not. The fields used for comfort are averaged over the last 10 minutes of the run.

No radiation and adiabatic walls. Surfaces do not exchange heat with the air or with each other, and there is no cold downdraught from glazing.

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you should be able to:

Explain why a low-energy house needs a modulating heat emitter that closely follows the heating demand.

Calculate the time constant of a light and a heavy floor from the build-up, and the heat the floor stores and still delivers after the loop closes.

Judge from the time constant whether a floor can follow a heating demand that changes over 24 hours (amplitude ratio and time lag).

Describe the control chain: heating curve, room temperature sensor, wax thermostat, on/off and PI control with PWM.

Compare light and heavy floors under on/off and PI control with PWM and different supply temperatures, on return temperature and deviation from the setpoint, using the control model.

Explain self-regulation and how a low supply temperature makes use of it, and use the control model to demonstrate self-regulation.

Calculate the required pre-settings for hydronic balancing, and explain why balancing matters for a low return temperature and what a high supply temperature does to the return temperature.

Floor heating is the standard heat emitter in newer Danish dwellings. It is invisible, it frees wall space, and it potentially works with very low supply temperatures, which suits heat pumps and district heating very well.

Warm water from a manifold runs through a pipe loop in the floor of each room and returns a few kelvin cooler. The heat first warms the floor, and the floor surface then gives it to the room by radiation and convection (

Figure 1).



Figure 1:Principle of hydronic floor heating. (a) One pipe loop per room, fed from a manifold. (b) Heat passes from the water into the slab, and from the floor surface to the room by radiation and convection. In a low-energy house the floor is only 1–3 K warmer than the room air.

In an older house with a large heat demand it gives good comfort, with warm feet and a small vertical temperature gradient.

A low-energy house is a different case. The heat loss is small, only 10 W per m² of floor at design conditions, and much less on an ordinary spring or autumn day. Solar and internal gains are large in comparison, and the heat that must be supplied is so small that it has to be delivered precisely. On a clear day in April a heating demand at night can turn into a surplus by noon. The heat emitter must therefore modulate: it must follow the demand closely, give less as soon as the gains rise, and nothing when they cover the loss.

A floor stores heat before it reaches the room, so its output follows the water with a delay. Water put into a heavy floor at 04:00 keeps warming the room after the sun has come out and the demand has gone. The heavier the floor, the longer the delay, and the harder it is to make the floor follow the demand.

This chapter judges how well, and when, floor heating suits low-energy houses. It uses four measures that apply to any heat emitter:

Heating energy. The heat delivered to the room. Heat that leaves through an open window must be paid for twice: once as heating energy, and again as discomfort.

Deviation from the setpoint. The time integral of the difference between the room temperature and the setpoint, in K·h. Time below the setpoint is discomfort. Time above it is heat the room did not need, which usually leaves through an open window.

Return temperature. The return water goes back to the heat source. A low return temperature lets a heat pump run at a lower condensing temperature, and in district heating it reduces the heat loss of the return pipes. It is weighted by the mass flow, because the heat source sees the mixed return of all loops.

Peak-to-average ratio. The peak hourly heat output divided by the mean output over the day. The heat source and the grid must be sized for the peak, and a heat pump runs most efficiently at a steady, low output. A ratio close to 1 means the emitter draws heat evenly.

The question for the designer is whether floor heating can meet these measures as well as a fast emitter, such as an electric panel radiator or air heating, which responds within minutes. The sections on build-up, time constant, hydronics and control explain the mechanisms. 

Control comparison puts them together and compares a light and a heavy floor under different controls and supply temperatures with a fast emitter.

Convection Convective heat transfer from a heated floor depends strongly on surface type, air speed, and forced or natural convection, but is about 6 W/(m²·K) for a heated floor.

Floor covering adds thermal resistance between the pipes and the room. Tiles add little, while wood and carpet add a lot, so a wooden floor needs a higher water temperature for the same output.

Floor heating constructions are often grouped by how the pipes are embedded, i.e. how much heat capacity sits between the pipes and the room (

Figure 3).

In a light (dry) floor the pipes lie in grooves in an insulation panel, usually EPS. Aluminium heat-diffusion plates wrap around the pipes and spread the heat sideways under the floor covering. The EPS panels rest on a plywood board on the joists, and the covering is laid directly on the plates, typically 22 mm floor boards, a floating wooden floor or gypsum fibre boards. Pipe spacing is anything between 150–300 mm, depending on pipe diameter and system.

Light floors are used on timber joists and battens, in renovation, and wherever build height and weight must be kept low. The whole construction above the insulation is 25–50 mm thick and weighs 10–30 kg/m². Its heat capacity above the pipes is about 15–30 kJ/(m²·K), so there is little heat to store.



Figure 4:A light floor before the floor boards are laid. The pipes lie in grooved boards under aluminium plates that spread the heat sideways. Photo: C. A. Hviid.

In a heavy floor the pipes are cast into cement screed or concrete. A typical screed system has 45–65 mm of screed above the pipes. In Danish slab-on-ground houses the pipes are often tied to the reinforcement in the middle of a 100 mm concrete slab, with the floor covering laid directly on the slab. The slab weighs around 230 kg/m² and has a heat capacity of 100–250 kJ/(m²·K), and all of it is heated by the pipes.



Figure 5:A heavy floor before the concrete is cast. The pipes are tied to the reinforcement mesh on top of the EPS insulation and end up in the middle of the slab. Photo: C. A. Hviid.

Several elements delay the floor’s response when the heat demand of the room changes:

Room temperature sensor and controller. The room must first deviate from the setpoint before the controller reacts.

Wax thermostat. The wax must warm up or cool down before the valve moves. This gives a dead time of a few minutes and a stroke of a few minutes more.

Water flow. At the low flow rates of floor heating the water takes several minutes to pass through a 100 m loop.

Heat capacity of the floor. The floor must be charged or discharged before its surface temperature changes. This is by far the longest delay, from about an hour in a light floor to many hours in a heavy floor.

The first three add minutes to tens of minutes. Only the heat capacity of the floor is large enough to matter over a day, and the rest of this section is about that.

A floor stores heat between the pipes and the room, so its output follows the water with a delay. The delay is measured by the floor’s time constant, \tau = RC: the heat capacity of the floor times the resistance from the floor to the room. It is the time the floor takes to complete 63 % of a change in output after the loop opens or closes. The number 63 % comes from the exponential response of a single heat store: after one time constant the remaining change has fallen to e^{-1} = 37\,\%. After three time constants 95 % of the change is complete. The time constant is also the time it would take to empty the store if the floor kept giving off heat at its initial rate. The derivation is in the dropdown at the end of this section. What matters here is the result, and whether a floor can deliver the heat when the room needs it.

The two floors give different outputs with the same water temperature, because the resistance from the water to the room is smaller in the heavy floor (pipes cast in concrete, thin parquet) than in the light floor (pipes under 22 mm boards). To give the same output, the light floor needs warmer water.

The last two rows are the ones that matter in a low-energy house. When the heavy floor’s loop closes, the slab still holds about 500 Wh/m² more heat than at room temperature, and it hands this heat to the room over the next day. If the house needs 5 W/m² on average on a spring day, that is about four days’ heating stored in the floor. The room overheats, and the heat must be removed again by opening windows or by cooling.

A light floor holds 70 Wh/m², 14 % of that heat, and most of it is released within the first hour. It follows the demand much better, but it still lags behind it, and the control loop adds more delay.

The heating demand of a low-energy house in early spring swings over the day, roughly as a sine with a 24-hour period, from a demand at night to a surplus when the sun shines. A floor with a time constant delivers only part of that swing, and delivers it delayed (

Table 2).



Figure 7:A first-order floor following a heating demand that swings over 24 hours, equation 

(7). The arrows mark the lag behind the demand peak at 04:00. Only the swing is shown; the daily mean is delivered in full. 

View script

The light floor follows the daily swing almost fully, one hour late (

Figure 7). The heavy floor flattens it to a third and shifts it by nearly five hours. Heat asked for at 04:00, the coldest hour, is delivered around 09:00, just as the sun takes over.

The figure shows only the swing around the daily mean. The heavy floor delivers the daily mean in full, but at 04:00 it delivers the mean plus only 30 % of the swing, so the room gets less than it needs and actually cools below the setpoint. To compensate, the room thermostat charges the slab further. The heavy floor therefore misses the setpoint in both directions: too cold at night and too warm in the afternoon. A lag of a quarter of the period, 6 h, is the worst case, because the floor then heats hardest when the demand is changing from heating to cooling.

Extra: what would it take for the floor to follow the demand?

Figure 8 turns the question around: how much heat must the water give for the floor to deliver exactly the demand? The light floor needs almost the demand itself, one hour early. The heavy floor needs a swing 3.3 times larger, nearly 5 hours early: 21 W/m² around 23:00, and −11 W/m² around 11:00. The water would have to cool the slab during the day, which a heating system cannot do, and the control would have to know the demand 5 hours ahead, for example from a weather forecast.



Figure 8:Heat the water must give for the floor output to follow a heating demand of 0–10 W/m² exactly, for a first-order floor with τ = 1 h and τ = 12 h. Below zero the water would have to cool the floor. 

View script

The lag is for the floor alone. The wax thermostat’s dead time and stroke, the room’s own heat capacity and the controller all add to it.

Several strategies reduce the problem, but none of them removes it:

Low supply temperature and self-regulation. With the supply only a few kelvin above the room, the floor delivers less when the room warms up, even with the valve open.

Heating stop and a broad deadband. Stop heating above an outdoor temperature limit, for example 12–15 °C, and use a broad deadband between the heating and cooling setpoints, so the room temperature can float more.

Anticipating the sun. Lower the setpoint in the morning on sunny days, using a weather forecast or model predictive control.

Shading and ventilative cooling. Remove the solar gain or the surplus heat (see Part D).

Floor cooling. The same pipes can cool by 20–40 W/m², limited by the dew point and a minimum floor surface temperature of about 19–20 °C. But the floor is just as slow when cooling.

The conclusion is that a low-energy house needs a heat emitter that modulates with the demand: its output must follow a demand that is small and changes within minutes. A light floor with a time constant of about 1 hour nearly does. A heavy floor with a time constant of about 12 hours does not, whatever the control. A fast emitter, such as an electric panel radiator or air heating, follows the demand even more closely.

Think of the floor above the insulation as one lump with heat capacity C [J/(m²·K)] and a single temperature T_f. When the loop closes, the only way out for the stored heat is through the floor covering and the floor surface, a total resistance R [m²·K/W], to the room at T_r.

Conservation of energy across lump boundaries (

Figure 9):



Figure 9:Energy balance of the floor as one lump. 

View script\dot E_{in} + \dot E_{gen} - \dot E_{out} = \dot E_{stored}

No heat is generated in the floor, and with the loop closed nothing comes in, so:\dot E_{stored} = - \dot E_{out}

Think of it as a tank with water, slowly losing heat through the insulated surface. Then the stored energy changes as temperature drops over time:\frac{m c_p\, \Delta T_f}{\Delta t} = - U A\, (T_f - T_r)C\,\frac{\mathrm{d}T_f}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\frac{T_f - T_r}{R}

The rate at which the floor cools is proportional to how much warmer it is than the room.

The solution to the equation is an exponential decay:T_f(t) - T_r = (T_{f,0} - T_r)\,e^{-t/\tau}, \qquad \tau = R\,C and since the heat output is $q = (T_f - T_r)/R$, the output decays the same way. A system that obeys {eq}`eq-lump-improved` is called first-order: one heat store, one resistance, one time constant. For any step change in the water flow, the output approaches its new value as

$$
q(t) = q_\infty + (q_0 - q_\infty)\,e^{-t/\tau}
$$ (eq-first-order-improved)
 

The time constant \tau has two useful meanings:

At t = \tau the factor e^{-1} = 0.37 remains, so 63 % of the change has happened. After 3\tau, 95 % has.

If the floor kept losing heat at its initial rate, it would be empty after exactly \tau. The initial slope of the curve points at t = \tau.The units confirm it: J/(m²·K) × m²·K/W = J/W = s.### Switching off: the whole floor discharges through the surface

When the loop closes, all the heat stored above the insulation has to leave through the flooring and the surface. C is the heat capacity of the whole floor above the insulation, and R is the flooring plus the surface resistance 1/h_s \approx 0.09 m²·K/W.

We calculate when 63% of the change has happened, i.e. when the floor temperature has dropped 63% of the way from initial T_f to ambient T_r:

Light floor: C \approx 18 kJ/(m²·K) for the boards and plates, R \approx 0.09 + 0.17 = 0.26 m²·K/W (22 mm boards, λ = 0.13 W/(m·K)), so \tau \approx 4700 s, or about 1.3 hours.

Heavy floor: C \approx 230 kJ/(m²·K) for the slab, R \approx 0.09 + 0.08 + 0.03 = 0.20 m²·K/W (surface, parquet, upper half of the slab), so \tau \approx 46\,000 s, or about 13 hours.

The flooring matters. A rug raises R, which lowers the output and slows the discharging of the floor.

Because \tau = R C, and R between pipes and floor is much smaller than between floor and ambient air, the time to heat up is much lower than to cool off.

A first-order system that is asked to follow a daily swing does two things: it lags behind, and it delivers less of the swing than asked, because demand starts dropping before the full output is reached.

Time Lag: The output peak lags behind the input peak.

Attenuation: The output amplitude is reduced.

For a diurnal cycle with a period of T = 24\text{ hours } (86{,}400\text{ s})

Ordinary Frequency (f): f = \frac{1}{T} = 0.0417\text{ cycles/hour}

Angular Frequency (\omega): \omega = 2\pi f = \frac{2\pi}{24\text{ h}} \approx 0.262\text{ rad/hour}

The system’s dynamic performance is governed by its amplitude ratio (the attenuation factor) and time lag (the temporal phase shift):\text{amplitude ratio} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (\omega\tau)^2}}, \qquad
\text{time lag} = \frac{\arctan(\omega\tau)}{\omega}

The product \omega\tau = 2\pi\,\tau/24\,\mathrm{h} compares the time constant with the length of the day. If the floor reacts quickly compared with the day (\omega\tau \ll 1), it keeps up: the amplitude ratio is close to 1 and the lag close to \tau. If it reacts slowly (\omega\tau \gg 1), the demand has already turned before the floor has warmed up. It then follows only a small part of the swing, and the lag approaches a quarter of the period, 6 h. For the light floor \omega\tau = 0.26; for the heavy floor \omega\tau = 3.1. The daily mean is always delivered in full; only the swing around it is damped and delayed.

Heat source. A heat pump or district heating. Floor heating needs a low supply temperature, typically 30–35 °C in a low-energy house, with 3–5 K between supply and return.

Mixing shunt. A circulation pump, a motorized two-way valve on the primary return and a bypass with a check valve. The more the two-way valve closes, the less water goes back to the heat source, and the more return water the pump draws through the bypass into the supply. This lowers the supply to the temperature set by the controller. The controller follows a heating curve, which raises the supply temperature as the outdoor temperature falls.

Manifold. Distributes water to one loop per room, or several loops in large rooms. Each loop should be at most 80–100 m long to keep the pressure drop reasonable. Flow meters or balancing valves on the supply side set the design flow in each loop, so that every room gets its share (hydronic balancing).

Wax thermostats and room temperature sensors. Each loop has a valve on the return side, opened and closed by a wax thermostat, an electrically heated wax actuator. The room temperature sensor switches it on and off, either directly or by pulse-width modulation (PWM). The valve only opens or closes the loop. It cannot change the water temperature.

What goes wrong without balancing. A loop that gets too much flow returns water that is almost as warm as the supply. The temperature drop \Delta\theta between supply and return falls, and the return temperature rises. The room with the short loop is heated fast and the room at the end of the long loop too slowly, and the usual response is to raise the supply temperature or the pump setting until the worst room is warm. Both make the other loops worse. A high return temperature lowers the efficiency of a heat pump, and in district heating it increases the heat loss of the return pipes and is often penalised in the tariff.

A high supply temperature gives a high return temperature

At a given flow, the difference between return and room temperature is a fixed fraction of the difference between supply and room temperature. A loop designed for 35/30 °C in a 20 °C room starts 15 K above the room and returns 10 K above it, a fraction of two thirds. With 45 °C supply and the same flow, the return is about 20 + 2/3 · 25 ≈ 37 °C: 10 K more on the supply gives about 7 K more on the return. Raising the supply temperature to make up for poor balancing therefore pushes the return temperature up twice.

The loops on a manifold are connected in parallel, so they all see the same pressure difference \Delta p between the supply and return manifold. The pressure drop in a loop grows with the square of the flow,\Delta p = \left(\frac{\dot m}{K}\right)^2 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \dot m = K\,\sqrt{\Delta p}

where K is the flow coefficient of the loop: the mass flow at a pressure drop of 1 bar. Manufacturers give the flow coefficient of a valve as K_v in m³/h at 1 bar. K for a whole loop combines the pipe and the valve. With the same \Delta p on all loops, each loop gets a flow proportional to its own K.

Short loops get too much water

A pipe’s resistance grows with its length, so with a constant friction factor K \propto 1/\sqrt{L}. A 50 m loop then takes \sqrt{2} = 1.4 times the flow of a 100 m loop, although it usually serves a smaller room and needs less.

Each loop has a design flow, set by its design heat output and a design temperature drop of typically 5 K, for example 35/30 °C. How to calculate it is covered in other courses.

Pre-setting. The valve on each loop has an adjustable throttle, the pre-setting, which sets its K_v. The installer chooses the pre-setting so that every loop gets its design flow at the same manifold pressure: long loops get a high pre-setting (open), short loops a low one (throttled). The pump sets the pressure, the pre-settings divide the flow between the loops, much like the accelerator and the gear in a car. The pre-settings must be set after the system has been filled and vented, because air in the loops changes their resistance.

Return temperature. Across floor types, a low supply temperature carries through to a low return temperature, and especially in light floors self-regulation always gives a low return temperature. There are concerns, however: rooms may need different amounts of heat, because of their orientation and their internal gains.

Peak-to-average ratio. Room control makes the load peaky: the peak hour is 5–14 times the daily mean, against about 2.5 for the ideal heater. PI control and the heating curve lower the ratio. Self-regulation gives the steadiest load, 1.5–1.9, because the floor takes heat whenever the room is cooler than the floor. The ratio is computed from hourly means, since a heat source serving many loops sees a smoother load than the PWM pulses of one loop.

A heavy floor does worse: it uses up to 57 % more heat and deviates up to 36 K·h more than the ideal heater, unless the supply temperature is kept low.

Figure 24 compares the heavy floor with two strategies. In the first, the supply is a constant 40 °C and a PI controller with PWM switches the loop to hold 21 °C. In the second, the supply is a constant 23 °C and the loop is always open: there is no room control at all, only self-regulation.

The main points:

Self-regulation alone holds the room. With the loop always open, the room stays between 20.9 and 23.0 °C on the cloudy day, closer to 21 °C than with PI control at 40 °C (20.6–23.6 °C). The water gives at most 5 W/m², more when the room is cool and less when it is warm.

Less heat, less overheating. The open loop uses about a fifth less heat than PI control at 40 °C.

A low and steady return temperature. At 23 °C the return stays at 22.3–23.3 °C. At 40 °C it rises from 22 to 24 °C each time the slab is charged.



Figure 24:Self-regulation of the heavy floor in the control model, setpoint 21 °C. Constant supply of 40 °C with PI control and PWM, and constant supply of 23 °C with the loop always open (no room control). a) Room temperature. b) Heat from the water to the floor, cut at 40 W/m². c) Heat flux at the floor surface; negative values mean that the floor takes heat from the room. d) Return temperature while the valve is open, with the flow-weighted mean over the cloudy day as thin lines. Default inputs otherwise.

Try it in the control model

Open the 

control model, select the heavy floor, tick Fixed design flow under Room control and set the heating curve slope to 0, so the supply temperature is constant.

Set the max supply temperature to 35 °C and then to 25 °C. How do the heat flux at the floor surface and the room temperature change on the cloudy day?

Lower the supply temperature further, to 23 °C and 22 °C. When does the room start to fall below the setpoint at night? What happens to the return temperature?

Repeat with the light floor. Why does a low supply temperature help the light floor less?

Take-aways for low-energy houses

Heating energy. A light floor with PI control uses only 11–14 % more heat than an ideal heater. A heavy floor uses 22–35 % more, because heat stored at night comes out when the sun already heats the room.

Deviation from the setpoint. In a heavy floor, keep the supply temperature low. The floor then limits its own output, and the room overheats less.

Return temperature. With PI control and the heating curve, floor heating returns the water 2–3.5 K above the setpoint, and with self-regulation only about 1.5 K, which suits a heat pump or district heating. On/off control at 40 °C supply loses this advantage in a light floor, with a return near 31 °C.

Peak-to-average ratio. Room control makes the load peaky, 5–14 times the daily mean. A low, steady supply temperature without room control gives the steadiest load, below 2.

In buildings with several floors or apartments, one riser pump often feeds a manifold on each floor, each through its own shunt (

Figure 25). The shunt pump circulates water through the floor loops. A thermostatic valve on the return limits the supply temperature: when the sensor bulb gets too warm, it throttles the water returned to the riser, so less hot water is drawn in and more return water is mixed back through the bypass. The check valve stops riser water from flowing backwards through the bypass into the return.



Figure 25:A riser with a riser pump feeding two floor heating manifolds, each through a shunt with its own pump, a 2-way thermostatic valve on the return and a check valve in the bypass. Three pumps in total. Only one floor loop per manifold is drawn.

The check valve in the bypass is spring loaded and needs a certain pressure difference to open. This becomes a problem in low-energy apartment buildings, where the floor loops need little heat but the riser pump keeps its pressure up (

Figure 26). At design load the shunts draw a large flow from the riser, and the riser pump runs at its design point A. In mild weather the thermostatic valves throttle, the flow drawn from the riser becomes small, and a constant-speed riser pump runs up its curve to almost its shut-off head (point B). The riser pressure then pushes against the bypass. Before any water can flow up through the bypass, the thermostatic valve must absorb both the riser pressure and the opening pressure of the check valve. The valve ends up almost closed with a large pressure across it, so it hunts and can be noisy, and until the check valve opens the floor loops get either too little flow or water that is too hot.

A riser pump in proportional-pressure mode lowers its head as the flow falls (point C), which makes the problem much smaller. A check valve with a low opening pressure also helps.



Figure 26:Riser pump at design (A) and at low load with constant speed (B) and proportional pressure (C). The shaded band is the opening pressure of the check valve, which the thermostatic valve must absorb on top of the riser pressure before water flows through the bypass. Example values: 45 kPa shut-off head, 600 l/h design flow, 10 kPa opening pressure.

For most of the twentieth century, domestic hot water was a small item in the heat budget of a Danish house. A typical older house with energy label D needs around 150 kWh of space heating per m² of floor area per year. Hot water adds 13 kWh/m², less than a tenth of the total.

Better houses have changed the picture (

Figure 1). Insulation, airtightness and heat recovery ventilation have cut the space heating demand of a passive house to 15 kWh/m², and of a house in the Danish low-energy class to about 10 kWh/m². The hot water demand has not changed, because it depends on the people living in the house and not on its envelope. A family takes the same showers in a passive house as in a house from 1965. In a passive house hot water is therefore close to half of the heat demand, and in a low-energy class house it is more than half.



Figure 1:Net heat demand for space heating and domestic hot water in three Danish house standards. The label D value is an estimate for a 150 m² house in the middle of the D band. The hot water demand is the Be18 calculation value of 250 L/m² per year heated from 10 °C to 55 °C 

Aggerholm, 2018. Losses from the tank and pipes are not included. 

View script

Hot water in Building Code

The Danish energy frame calculation (Be18) uses a fixed hot water demand of 250 L per m² of heated floor area per year, heated from 10 °C to 55 °C 

Aggerholm, 2018. With the average properties of water between 10 °C and 55 °C this isQ = \bar\rho\,V\,\bar c_p\,(\theta - \theta_c) = \frac{994 \cdot 0.250 \cdot 4.182 \cdot (55 - 10)}{3600} = 13.0 \text{ kWh/(m}^2\,\text{year)}

For a 150 m² house it amounts to 2000 kWh per year, or about 100 L of 55 °C water per day which is a reasonable figure for a family of three or four.

However, measured hot water use varies by a factor of two or three between households of the same size, and it depends much more on the number of occupants, their age and their habits than on the floor area. The temperature also matters. A floor heating system in a low-energy house runs at 30–35 °C (Chapter C1). Hot water must be stored at 50–55 °C or more to keep Legionella bacteria from growing. When the same heat pump supplies both, the hot water is the expensive part of its work, because the efficiency of a heat pump falls as the temperature it delivers rises. In an all-electric low-energy house, hot water can easily use as much electricity as space heating.

There are two ways to cut the cost of hot water, and this chapter is built around them:

- **Use less heat.** Shower water leaves the house at about 30 °C, at the same moment as cold water comes in. A drain water heat recovery unit passes that heat to the incoming cold water. This is Part A of the chapter.
- **Buy the heat at the right time.** Electricity prices vary over the day, with a peak in the early evening, which is exactly when many families shower. A well-sized hot water tank can be charged in cheap hours and emptied in expensive ones. This is Part B.

The next section sets out how much hot water a dwelling uses and how fast it is drawn, which both parts build on.

The heat needed to warm a mass m of water from the cold water temperature \theta_c to the temperature \theta at the tap isQ = m\,c_p\,(\theta - \theta_c)

where m = \rho\,V. Both the density \rho and the specific heat capacity c_p of water vary with temperature. Between 10 °C and 55 °C the density falls from 999.7 to 985.7 kg/m³, while c_p stays close to 4.18 kJ/(kg·K). For hot water calculations we use the averages over that range, \bar\rho = 994 kg/m³ and \bar c_p = 4.182 kJ/(kg·K). One litre of water warmed by 1 K then takes 4.16 kJ, or 1.15 Wh. The cold water from Danish waterworks is about 8–10 °C as a yearly average, with a seasonal swing from around 5 °C in late winter to 15 °C in late summer.

At the tap, the user mixes hot water from the tank with cold water to get the temperature they want, typically 38–40 °C for a shower and 45 °C for washing up. The fraction of hot water in the mix follows from an energy balance:f_h = \frac{\theta_{mix} - \theta_c}{\theta_h - \theta_c}

With the tank at 55 °C and cold water at 10 °C, a 40 °C shower is two-thirds hot water and one-third cold. Equation 

(2) gives the same energy whether it is applied to the mixed water at 40 °C or to the hot water fraction at 55 °C, so either can be used. What matters is to be clear which one a consumption figure refers to. Water use statistics are usually given at the tap, while calculation standards usually give litres at 55 °C or 60 °C.

The energy per day is modest. The power during a tapping is not. The heat flow needed to warm water flowing at a volume flow \dot V is\Phi = \rho\,\dot V\,c_p\,(\theta - \theta_c)

Table 1 shows the energy and the power for some typical tappings. A shower at 8 L/min needs about 17 kW while it runs, and filling a bath needs about 25 kW.

Figure 2 shows a day of tappings for a family of four. Each tapping lasts only minutes, but a shower draws 15 kW while it runs. The whole day adds up to only 5.7 kWh. The tank simulator in 

Appendix E: Stratified tank simulator contains more tapping profiles: the EN 16147 test cycles, the statistical IEA SHC Task 26 profiles, profiles measured in Danish houses and a few illustrative ones, each with its source.

These powers are far larger than anything else in the heating system of a low-energy house. The whole house may need only 2–3 kW of space heating on the coldest day, and a heat pump sized for that cannot heat a shower as it runs. There are two ways out:

Instantaneous heating. District heating can deliver 30–40 kW through a heat exchanger in a flat station, so the water is heated as it is used and nothing is stored.

Storage. A heat pump or a small boiler heats a tank slowly, over hours, and the tank delivers the high power during the tapping. The tank decouples the power the heat source must deliver from the power the user draws. Storage is what makes it possible to choose *when* the heat source runs, which is the topic of Part B. Showers are what make drain water heat recovery worthwhile, which is the topic of Part A. They are the largest single hot water use in most homes, and they are the one use where the warm waste water flows to the drain at the same moment as the cold water comes in.
 

Rules of thumb

The cold water temperature is on average 10 C, which is ok for most calculations, but actually fluctuates between 8-17 C throughout the year.

1 L of water warmed by 1 K takes about 1.15 Wh. 100 L warmed by 45 K takes about 5 kWh.

One 8-minute shower uses about 60 L of 40 °C water, which is 40 L of 55 °C water and about 2 kWh of heat.

Hot water use is about 30–40 L of 55 °C water per person per day, or about 550–750 kWh per person per year before losses.

The Be18 calculation value is 13 kWh/m² per year, about 2000 kWh per year for a 150 m² house.

A shower draws about 15–20 kW while it runs, several times the design heat load of a low-energy house.

Four types of hot water heater are common in Danish single-family houses. They differ in where the heat comes from and in what else the unit does.

Electric water heater. A tank with an electric heating element and a thermostat. Each kWh of hot water costs one kWh of electricity, plus the standing loss of the tank, which is set by the insulation and the tank temperature. The electric water heater is the reference for the other solutions in this book.

Example: Metro Therm water heaters

The range runs from 14 to 288 L, insulated with polyurethane foam, with a thermostat that can be set up to about 65 °C 

Metro Therm, 2026.

Hot water heat pump. A tank with a small air-to-water heat pump on top. The heat pump takes its air through ducts, either outdoor air or exhaust air from the house. The COP at an air temperature of 20 °C is typically around 3 to 4. With outdoor air, the COP falls in winter, when the air is cold. With exhaust air, the heat source is close to room temperature all year, but the air flow is limited by the ventilation.

Example: MetroAir Aqua

The MetroAir Aqua heats a tank of 190 or 260 L with 1.6 kW of heat pump capacity. The COP is 3.7 and 4.1 at an air temperature of 20 °C for the two tank sizes 

Nathan, 2025.

Heat pump for space heating and hot water. An air-to-water or ground source heat pump that serves both the floor heating and a hot water tank, often built into the indoor unit. The heat pump switches between floor heating at about 35 °C and charging the tank at 50–55 °C. The COP is lower when it heats hot water than when it heats the floor, because the condensing temperature is higher. The share of the year’s heat that goes to hot water grows as the space heating demand falls, so in a low-energy house the COP for hot water matters as much as the SCOP for space heating.

Example: Kronoterm Adapt 2

An air-to-water heat pump with an outdoor unit of 2 to 18 kW and the natural refrigerant R290. The SCOP is up to 6.22 at a flow temperature of 35 °C (EN 14825, average climate), and the flow temperature can reach 75 °C 

Kronoterm, 2026. With the HYDRO C2 indoor unit, the hot water tank is built into the indoor unit.

Compact unit. A compact unit combines balanced ventilation with heat recovery, an exhaust-air heat pump and a hot water tank in one cabinet. The heat pump takes heat from the exhaust air after the heat exchanger and uses it for the hot water and, in some units, the supply air. The heat source is limited by the ventilation air flow, so the unit suits houses with a small heating demand, such as passive houses. Because ventilation, heat pump and tank share one cabinet, the parts are harder to reach and replace than in separate units, and a fault in one part can take ventilation and hot water out of service together.

Example: Nilan Compact P

The Compact P has a 180 L tank in a cabinet of 900 × 610 × 2065 mm. The counterflow heat exchanger has a temperature efficiency of up to 95 % 

Nilan, 2026. The unit is certified as a Passive House component at air flows of 

92 m³/h and 

172 m³/h.

The Danish Energy Agency keeps an official list of heat pumps sold in Denmark, Varmepumpelisten, with the tested efficiency of each product 

Energistyrelsen, 2026. It is the place to compare heat pumps of the types above.REVIEW LATER (Christian, 2026-10-16): check the note on servicing compact units such as the Nilan Compact P. The MetroAir Aqua data are for the 201 and 301 models; check them against the 202 and 302 in the link.

A hot water tank loses heat to the room around it all the time, whether or not water is drawn. This standing loss is set by the insulation and by the temperature difference between the tank and the room. For a tank at a uniform temperature \theta with heat capacity C = \rho c_p V and heat loss coefficient UA, the energy balance without tapping and charging isC \frac{d\theta}{dt} = -UA\,(\theta - \theta_a)

where \theta_a is the room temperature. From a start temperature \theta_0, the tank cools exponentially with the time constant \tau = C/UA,\theta(t) = \theta_a + (\theta_0 - \theta_a)\,e^{-t/\tau}

and the heat lost after the time t is Q(t) = C\,(\theta_0 - \theta(t)).

Water heaters and hot water tanks sold in the EU carry an energy label. The label class is set by the standing loss S in W, measured with the tank at 65 °C in a room at 20 °C, and the class limits grow with the volume as V^{0.4} 

European Commission, 2013. Since 2017, a tank of up to 2000 L may only be sold if it is in class C or better

A household on an hourly contract pays the spot price of the hour plus a set of fixed and time-dependent charges. In eastern Denmark (DK2) in 2026, the price per kWh isp(t) = \big(p_{spot}(t) + p_{net}(t) + p_{TSO} + p_{tax}\big)\,(1 + 0.25)

where p_{spot} is the day-ahead price of the hour, p_{net} the network tariff of the local grid company, p_{TSO} Energinet’s system and network tariffs (7.2 + 4.3 øre/kWh 

Energinet, 2025), p_{tax} the electricity tax and 0.25 the VAT. The electricity tax was 72.7 øre/kWh until 2025. In 2026 and 2027 it is cut to the EU minimum of 0.8 øre/kWh 

Skatteministeriet, 2025, which makes the hourly part of the price far more important than before.

Two of the terms change over the day (

Figure 4):

The spot price follows the balance between demand and wind and solar production. On a typical weekday it has one peak in the morning and a higher one at 17–20, when people come home and cook and solar production falls away. It is lowest at night and, on sunny days, at midday.

The network tariff is a fixed time-of-use tariff. Radius charges, in winter (October to March), 11 øre/kWh at 00–06, 32 øre/kWh at 06–17 and 21–24, and 96 øre/kWh at the peak 17–21. In summer, the peak tariff is less than half of that 

Bolius, 2026.

The two peaks coincide. On the day in 

Figure 4, the consumer price runs from 1.17 DKK/kWh at 03:00 to 4.68 DKK/kWh at 19:00, a factor of four. The family of four draws 57 % of its hot water heat at 06–08 and 37 % at 17–21, in the most expensive hours of the day. Heated as it is used, its hot water costs on average 2.38 DKK/kWh of electricity. This is the price weighted by the hot water heat drawn in each hour, and it is higher than the daily average of 1.89 DKK/kWh. Heated at night, 00–06, it costs 1.22 DKK/kWh, half as much.

Over a year, the saving is of the order of a few thousand DKK with a resistance heater and about a thousand DKK with a heat pump.

The primary energy factor and CO₂ over the day

records.content:
The Danish energy frame (BR18) uses one fixed primary energy factor for electricity, 1.9. The real factor changes from hour to hour with the production mix. Each source i gets a non-renewable primary energy factor, and the factor of the mix in hour t isf_{P,nren}(t) = \frac{\sum_i E_i(t)\, f_{P,nren,i}}{\sum_i E_i(t)}

where E_i(t) is the electricity from source i in hour t. Wind and solar have a non-renewable factor of zero. Fossil plants have a factor close to 1/\eta. The CO₂ intensity behaves the same way, and for this reason it serves as a proxy for CO₂ in this book.

Danish electricity emitted on average 124 g CO₂-eq/kWh in 2025, counted on consumption and including imports. Single hours ranged from 36 to 363 g/kWh. In winter, the average day goes from 130 g/kWh at 01:00 to 166 g/kWh at 16:00, and in summer from 81 to 100 g/kWh 

Electricity Maps, 2026. Price and CO₂ often point the same way, because the expensive evening hours are also the hours with more fossil production and imports. But they are not the same signal. A windy afternoon can be cheap and clean while the night after it is calm and dirty. A charging strategy that follows the price is therefore not automatically the one with the lowest CO₂.

For hand calculations, the hourly data can be reduced to a few periods of the day. Scale the BR18 factor by the mean CO₂ intensity c of each period, relative to the daily mean \bar c, weighted by the length of each period:f_{P}(t) = 1.9\,\frac{c(t)}{\bar c}

Figure 5 shows the result for Denmark in 2021, in four periods of the day. The night, 22–06, gets a factor of 1.66, the day, 06–17, 2.05, and the evening, 17–22, 1.95. Averaged over the 24 hours, the factor is 1.9. The spread is only about ±10 % around 1.9, much smaller than the spread in price, which is why a charging strategy saves far more money than primary energy.REVIEW LATER (Christian, 2026-10-14): the periods 17-22 and 22-24 do not match the Radius tariff periods 17-21 and 21-24. hierarchy.lvl2: Sizing the tank as a thermal battery
Sizing the tank as a thermal battery

records.content:
A hot water tank is a battery for heat. When it is charged, the heat source runs. When hot water is drawn, the tank delivers. If the tank is big enough, the two no longer have to happen at the same time, and the heat pump can run in the hours when electricity is cheap or has a low primary energy factor. The question is how big “big enough” is.

The heat a fully charged tank holds, counted from the cold water temperature, isQ_{tank} = \bar\rho\,V\,\bar c_p\,(\theta_{set} - \theta_c)

Not all of it can be used. Between the hot water at the top and the cold water at the bottom there is a mixing zone, the thermocline, and water from that zone is too cold for a shower. The tank is “empty” for the user long before all of it is at \theta_c. We account for this with a usable fraction \eta_{use}, typically 0.8–0.9 for a well-stratified tank and lower for a tank that mixes when it is charged.

The method compares, hour by hour, the heat the tank has to deliver with the heat the charging strategy puts in. It is the same method used to size water reservoirs, and it needs nothing more than a spreadsheet with one row per hour.

Step 1. Hourly heat demand. From the tapping profile, add up the heat drawn in each hour, Q = \rho\,V\,c_p\,(\theta - \theta_c), using the volume and use temperature of each tapping. Add the standing loss of the tank as a constant amount per hour, \Phi_{loss} = UA\,(\theta_{set} - \theta_{room}). The sum over the day is the heat the tank must receive, Q_{day}.

Step 2. Hourly charging. Spread Q_{day} evenly over the hours the charging strategy allows. With N allowed hours, the heat source must deliver \Phi_{ch} = Q_{day}/N during those hours. This is the first check of the design: if \Phi_{ch} is larger than the heat output of the heat pump, the strategy cannot work, whatever the tank size.

Step 3. Cumulative curves. Add up the demand and the charging hour by hour, and plot both cumulative curves over the day. The difference between them, charge minus demand, is the change in the heat stored in the tank since midnight. The tank must never hold less than nothing, so lift the charge curve until it just touches the demand curve from above. The largest vertical gap between the two curves is then the heat the tank must store, Q_{store}. In a spreadsheet, this is simply the maximum minus the minimum of the column “cumulative charge − cumulative demand”.

Step 4. Volume. Solve equation 

(10) for the volume, with the usable fraction:V = \frac{Q_{store}}{\bar\rho\,\bar c_p\,(\theta_{set} - \theta_c)\,\eta_{use}}

Round up to the next standard tank size.

The method is a first estimate. It assumes the tank is either hot or cold, with a fixed usable fraction, and that the heat source charges evenly over its allowed hours. In a real tank, the thermocline grows while the tank sits, the heat pump is switched by a thermostat at a sensor partway up the tank, and the standing loss depends on how much of the tank is hot. The tank simulator in 

Appendix E: Stratified tank simulator handles all of this, so the hand estimate should always be checked there.

A family of four uses the profile “Family of 4, morning and evening” from the tank simulator (

Appendix E: Stratified tank simulator): two showers at 06:30–07:00, one at 20:00, and small tappings during the day. Three showers a day, rather than one per person, matches the Be18 calculation value for a 150 m² house; measured Danish households shower even less 

Marszal-Pomianowska & others, 2021. The tank is kept at 55 °C, the cold water is 10 °C, and the tank has UA = 1.2 W/K in a room at 20 °C. How large a tank is needed if the heat pump may run only between 00:00 and 06:00? How large is it with uniform charging over the whole day?

Step 1. The tappings add up to 5.73 kWh per day. Of that, 2.91 kWh is drawn between 06:00 and 07:00 and 1.45 kWh between 20:00 and 21:00. The standing loss is 1.2 \cdot (55 - 20) = 42 W, or 1.01 kWh per day. So Q_{day} = 6.74 kWh.

Step 2. With night charging, N = 6 h and \Phi_{ch} = 6.74/6 = 1.12 kW. With uniform charging, \Phi_{ch} = 6.74/24 = 0.28 kW. Both are well within the 3 kW of a small heat pump - as long as the heatpump is not tasked with space heating also.

Step 3. 

Figure 6 shows the cumulative curves. With night charging, the tank receives all of the day’s heat by 06:00, before any hot water has been used. The gap is largest at 06:00, just before the morning showers: Q_{store} = 6.49 kWh. With uniform charging, the charge curve has to be lifted by 1.34 kWh so that it stays above the demand after the morning showers, where the two curves touch at 08:00. The gap is largest at 06:00, just before the two morning showers: Q_{store} = 2.77 kWh. With one shower in the evening, the morning peak is now the one that sets the size.



Figure 6:Cumulative charge and cumulative demand for the family of four, with uniform charging (left) and night charging 00–06 (right). The largest vertical gap is the heat the tank must store.

In both cases the hand estimate is close: the tank it gives delivers every shower at full temperature and falls just short only for one small kitchen tapping right after a peak. One standard size up, it is safe. A smaller tank fails where the method says it will, at the peak that sets the size. Note that the night-charged tank loses less than half of the standing loss we assumed, because it is cold for much of the evening. The uniform case works for a different reason than the method assumes: the heat pump does not charge evenly at 0.28 kW. A thermostat starts it at full power when the sensor has cooled, and during the morning showers its 3 kW output helps cover the draw.

Rules of thumb

1 kWh stored at 55 °C, counted from 10 °C cold water, needs about 20 L of water, or 23 L with a usable fraction of 0.85.

Charging only at night means storing a full day of hot water: about 40–45 L per person.

Charging whenever needed, with a thermostat, needs about 20–25 L per person, enough to cover the largest peak.

The heat pump must deliver at least the daily heat divided by the number of allowed hours, plus a margin.

In an apartment building, hot water is produced centrally, in a district heating substation with a tank or a plate heat exchanger, and distributed to the flats through risers. Without circulation, the water in a riser cools between tappings, and the user has to run the tap until hot water arrives. A circulation loop prevents this. A pump keeps the hot water moving through the supply pipes and back to the substation, so that the whole network stays hot at all hours. The return of the loop is kept above 50 °C to limit the growth of Legionella.

The heat lost from the circulation pipes is\Phi_{circ} = \sum_j \frac{L_j\,(\theta_{w,j} - \theta_{a,j})}{R'_j}

where L_j is the length of pipe section j, \theta_{w,j} the water temperature, \theta_{a,j} the surrounding air temperature and R'_j the thermal resistance per metre of insulated pipe. The loss runs 8760 hours a year, whether hot water is used or not.

Measurements show that the loss is large. In Danish apartment buildings, circulation losses were 23–70 % of the heat delivered to the hot water system, and 54–89 % in office buildings 

Bøhm, 2013. In 134 Swedish multi-family buildings, the measured loss ranged from 0.5 to 76 kWh per m² of heated floor area per year. The mean was 14 kWh/m² in older buildings and 6 kWh/m² in newer ones, against an assumed 4 kWh/m² 

Burke et al., 2020.

When you take a shower, about 8 L of water at 40 °C leaves the shower head every minute. A few seconds later the same water runs down the drain at 35–38 °C, having lost only a few kelvin on its way through the air and over your skin. At the same moment, 8 L of cold water at about 10 °C enters the house to replace it. A drain water heat recovery unit is a heat exchanger between these two flows. It needs no storage, no pump and no control, because the two flows are there at the same time and stop at the same time. It only works for tappings with that property, and in a home that means showers. A bath is filled first and emptied later, and a kitchen sink or a washbasin draws little water at a time.

Figure 1 shows a vertical unit installed in a basement and how it is connected in a house.



Figure 1:A vertical drain water heat recovery unit. Left: installed in a basement; the copper coil around the drain carries the cold water upwards. Photo: Recycle9876, 

Wikimedia Commons, public domain. Right: connected so that the preheated water feeds both the shower and the water heater (equal flow, connection 3 below). Diagram: Ashp uk, 

Wikimedia Commons, 

CC BY-SA 4.0.

Figure 2 shows the two main types.

Vertical units replace about 1.5–2 m of the vertical drain pipe below the shower. The inner pipe is copper. Water falling down a vertical pipe does not fill it, but spreads into a thin film that clings to the wall, so almost all of the copper surface is wetted by a thin, fast-moving layer of warm water. The cold water flows upwards in a coil or a narrow annulus around the pipe, in counterflow to the drain water. This is a good heat exchanger, and the best vertical units recover 70 % of the heat that could at most be recovered. The catch is that a vertical unit needs a storey of straight vertical drain below the shower, which means a basement or a floor below. It suits a house with a basement and an apartment block where the bathrooms are stacked.

Horizontal units sit in the floor, under a shower tray or in a channel drain. They fit a slab-on-ground house and a bathroom renovation. In a channel drain, the heat exchanger is a row of copper tubes along the bottom of the channel, with the cold water flowing inside them against the direction of the drain water. The drain water flows around and over the tubes in a shallow layer. The unit is short, typically 0.7–0.9 m, and the water in the channel moves slowly, so it has less length and less turbulence to give off its heat than the falling film in a vertical pipe. Some manufacturers add turbulators between the tubes to stir the flow. The lower the shower flow, the thinner the water layer around the tubes and the higher the effectiveness. The better horizontal units still reach about 60 %.



Figure 2:A vertical unit (left) and a horizontal unit in a shower channel drain (right). Temperatures are for an 8 L/min shower with equal flow on both sides, an effectiveness of 0.70 for the vertical unit and 0.50 for the horizontal one. 

View script

Both types must keep the drinking water safe if the wall between the two flows fails. Certified units therefore have a double wall with a vented gap between the drain water and the drinking water, so a leak shows up as water dripping out of the gap rather than as sewage in the drinking water. The drain side gets a film of soap, skin fat and hair over time. A vertical unit is largely self-cleaning, because the falling water scours the wall, while a horizontal unit needs the grate and the channel cleaned as part of normal bathroom cleaning. On the cold side, the unit adds a pressure loss of about 0.1–0.4 bar at shower flow.

How good a unit is, is expressed by its effectiveness: the heat it actually transfers, divided by the most heat that could be transferred.

The most that could be transferred is the heat that would cool the drain water all the way down to the cold water temperature, or warm the cold water all the way up to the drain water temperature, whichever flow has the smaller heat capacity rate C = \rho\,\dot V\,c_p.

When the two flows are equal (connection 3 below), the heat flow transferred [W] is\Phi = \varepsilon\, C\,(\theta_d - \theta_c)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\varepsilon = \frac{\theta_p - \theta_c}{\theta_d - \theta_c}

where \theta_d is the drain water temperature entering the unit, \theta_c the cold water temperature and \theta_p the temperature of the preheated cold water leaving it.

With drain water at 37 °C, cold water at 10 °C and \varepsilon = 0.6, the cold water leaves the unit at \theta_p = 10 + 0.6 \cdot 27 = 26 °C.

The Passive House Institute certifies drain water heat recovery units at equal flow on both sides, 8 L/min, and sorts them into efficiency classes from phA+ to phC 

Passive House Institute, 2026.

An alternative source is the 

searchable product list of Natural Resources Canada 

Natural Resources Canada, 2026. It lists many more units, mostly vertical ones from North American makers, tested to the Canadian standard CSA B55.1. For each unit it gives the heat recovery efficiency (the same quantity as the effectiveness here), the heat recovery rate in kW, the length and diameter, and an energy credit for two shower flows. The test conditions differ from the Passive House test, so compare units within one list, not across the two.

The ε-NTU method is used when the two flows are not equal.

Then, a heat exchanger is described by two numbers. The heat capacity ratio compares the two flows,C_r = \frac{C_{min}}{C_{max}}, \qquad C = \rho\,\dot V\,c_p

and the number of transfer units compares the heat transfer surface with the smaller flow,NTU = \frac{UA}{C_{min}}

where UA is the overall heat transfer coefficient times the area, in W/K. A large NTU means a large surface for the flow it has to heat.

For a counterflow heat exchanger, the effectiveness follows from these two numbers alone:\varepsilon = \frac{1 - \exp\left[-NTU\,(1 - C_r)\right]}{1 - C_r\,\exp\left[-NTU\,(1 - C_r)\right]}

and the heat transferred is \Phi = \varepsilon\,C_{min}\,(\theta_d - \theta_c).

When the flows are equal, C_r = 1, then equation 

(4) becomes 0/0. Taking the limit C_r \to 1 gives the much simpler\varepsilon = \frac{NTU}{1 + NTU}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
NTU = \frac{\varepsilon}{1 - \varepsilon}

The second form turns a certified effectiveness into the size of the heat exchanger. A unit certified at \varepsilon = 0.60 at 8 L/min has NTU = 0.60/0.40 = 1.5, so its UA equals the heat capacity rate of 12 L/min of water.

Now feed the same unit with unequal flows. Take the shower from before, 8 L/min at 40 °C with drain water at 37 °C and cold water at 10 °C, but connect the unit so that the preheated water goes only to the cold inlet of the shower mixer (connection 1 in 

Figure 3 below). The water heater delivers 55 °C and is still fed with cold mains water.

Step 1: the mixer sets the cold-side flow. All 8 L/min go down the drain, but only the cold part of the shower water passes the unit. A thermostatic mixer blends a flow \dot V_h of hot water at 55 °C with a flow \dot V_p of preheated water at \theta_p, so that the mix is 40 °C. A mass and energy balance on the mixer gives\dot V_h + \dot V_p = 8 \text{ L/min}, \qquad
\dot V_h \cdot 55 + \dot V_p\,\theta_p = 8 \cdot 40
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\dot V_p = 8\,\frac{55 - 40}{55 - \theta_p} \text{ L/min}

The warmer the preheated water, the more of it the mixer takes. Without the unit, \theta_p = 10 °C and \dot V_p = 2.67 L/min. With \theta_p = 30 °C, \dot V_p = 4.8 L/min.

Step 2: the heat exchanger sets the preheat temperature. The drain side carries 8 L/min and the cold side \dot V_p, so the cold side has the smaller heat capacity rate, C_{min} = \rho c_p \dot V_p.

The size of the unit, UA, comes from its certificate: \varepsilon = 0.60 at equal flows of 8 L/min gives NTU = 1.5, so UA = 1.5 \cdot \rho c_p \cdot 8 = \rho c_p \cdot 12 L/min.

It is convenient to write UA as the heat capacity rate of 12 L/min of water, because \rho c_p then cancels in NTU. UA is assumed unchanged, since the drain side still carries the 8 L/min of the test. ThenNTU = \frac{12}{\dot V_p}, \qquad C_r = \frac{\dot V_p}{8}

and equation 

(4) gives \varepsilon. The effectiveness then gives the preheat temperature. The heat transferred can be written in two ways: from the definition of effectiveness, and as the heat picked up by the cold water, which warms from \theta_c to \theta_p:\Phi = \varepsilon\,C_{min}\,(\theta_d - \theta_c) = C_{cold}\,(\theta_p - \theta_c)

Here the cold side is the smaller flow, C_{cold} = C_{min}, so C_{min} cancels:\theta_p = \theta_c + \varepsilon\,(\theta_d - \theta_c) = 10 + \varepsilon \cdot (37 - 10)

This is the same expression as for equal flows in equation 

(1). It holds whenever the cold side is the smaller flow. If the cold side were the larger flow, C_{min} would be the drain side, and the cold water would be heated by only \varepsilon\,C_r\,(\theta_d - \theta_c).

Step 3: solve the two together. Equation 

(6) needs \theta_p to give the flow, and step 2 needs the flow to give \theta_p. The simplest way is to guess \theta_p, compute the flow, compute a new \theta_p, and repeat (

Table 2). The first guess, no preheat, gives a small flow, which the large unit heats almost to the drain temperature. That makes the mixer take much more preheated water in the next round, which is then heated less. The guesses swing back and forth around the answer and settle after about eight rounds.

The preheated water can go to three places (

Figure 3):

To the cold side of the shower mixer only. The water heater is still fed with cold mains water.

To the water heater only. The shower mixer is still fed with cold mains water.

To both. All the water that ends up in the shower has passed through the unit, so the flow on the cold side equals the flow down the drain. This is called equal flow or balanced connection.
