The heater must still be sized for the shower without the unit, 16.6 kW, for two reasons. The unit only preheats once warm water reaches the drain, so at the start of every shower the heater gets cold water. All other taps, and a bath, get no preheat at all. The unit therefore lowers the energy but not the installed power. That matters for an instantaneous electric water heater, which at these powers needs a three-phase supply. A tank or a district heating heat exchanger covers the peak anyway.

hierarchy.lvl3: Effectiveness increases with lower shower flow
Effectiveness increases with lower shower flow

records.content:
A unit with \varepsilon = 0.70 has NTU = 0.70/0.30 = 2.3, and one with \varepsilon = 0.41 has NTU = 0.7. When the shower flow rises, C rises in proportion. UA also rises, because faster water transfers heat better, but less than in proportion. So NTU falls, and the effectiveness with it. 

Figure 4 (left) shows this for the two units of 

Table 1, assuming UA grows with the square root of the flow. A low-flow shower head therefore saves twice: it uses less hot water, and the unit recovers a larger share of the heat in the water that is used.

Figure 4 (right) shows the saving for all three connections over the range of certified effectiveness. The balanced connection is always best. For units with a low effectiveness, connection 2 (to the water heater) is slightly better than connection 1; for the best units it is the other way round. In practice the choice is often made by the pipe layout. Connection 1 needs only a short pipe from the unit to the shower mixer, and connection 2 needs a pipe from the unit to the water heater, which may be far away. Connection 3 needs both, and it is the one to aim for in a new building.



Figure 4:Left: effectiveness at equal flow against shower flow for the two units in 

Table 1, from the certified value at 8 L/min with UA proportional to the square root of the flow. Right: share of the shower heat saved for the three connections, with the two units marked, for an 8 L/min shower at 40 °C, drain water at 37 °C and cold water at 10 °C. 

View script

The annual saving is the shower heat times the saving fraction:Q_{saved} = s\,Q_{shower}

where Q_{shower} is the heat for showers over the year, Q = \rho\,V\,c_p\,(\theta_{mix} - \theta_c) summed over all showers. Showers are the largest single use of hot water in most homes, typically half to two-thirds of the hot water heat. One 8-minute shower at 8 L/min and 40 °C takes 2.2 kWh (

Table 1). A person who showers on three days out of four uses about 600 kWh a year for showers, and a balanced unit with \varepsilon = 0.5 saves 45 % of that, about 270 kWh per person per year.

The saving varies over the year with the cold water temperature. With cold water at 5 °C in late winter, the unit with \varepsilon = 0.5 warms it by 16 K; at 15 °C in late summer, by 11 K. The fraction saved hardly changes (equation  gives 46 % and 44 %), because the shower also needs more heat in winter.

What the saved heat is worth depends on how the water is heated. With an electric resistance heater, every kWh of heat saved is a kWh of electricity saved. With a heat pump that delivers hot water at a COP of 3, it is only 0.33 kWh of electricity. Drain water heat recovery therefore pays back about three times faster in a house with an electric water heater than in a heat pump house. In a heat pump house, it competes with the heat pump: both are ways of not buying the same kWh of heat.

Drain water heat recovery also helps when the tank is used as a thermal battery, as in 

Domestic hot water. It cuts the heat drawn from the tank during each shower, by about half with a good balanced unit, so the tank needs to store less heat to cover the evening showers from a charge in cheap hours. A smaller tank also has a smaller standing loss. :::{admonition} Rules of thumb
:class: tip

- Certified units have an effectiveness of 0.4–0.7 at 8 L/min. The best vertical and horizontal units are not far apart, but the spread within each type is large.
- Effectiveness falls as the flow rises: about 0.05 lower at 12 L/min than at 8 L/min.
- With equal flow, a unit saves about 0.9 times its effectiveness of the shower heat. Feeding only the mixer or only the water heater saves about a sixth less.
- A good balanced unit saves 200–300 kWh of heat per person per year.
- A saved kWh of heat is worth a kWh of electricity with a resistance heater, but only about 0.33 kWh with a heat pump.
:::

records.content:
A family of four in a 150 m² house takes three showers a day, the same as in the tank sizing example in 

Domestic hot water. Each shower lasts 8 minutes at 8 L/min and 40 °C, and the cold water is 10 °C on average. They are rebuilding the bathroom and consider two options:

A. A Joulia-Inline 5 channel drain (\varepsilon = 0.41), connected to the shower mixer only, because the water heater is on the other side of the house (connection 1).

B. A Showersave QB1-21XE vertical unit (\varepsilon = 0.70) in the basement below the bathroom, connected to both the mixer and the water heater (connection 3).

How much heat and electricity does each save per year, with an electric water heater and with a heat pump at a COP of 3? What are the simple paybacks with electricity at 1.2 DKK/kWh?

Shower heat. One shower takes 64 \cdot 1.155 \cdot (40 - 10) = 2\,217 Wh. Three a day for a year is 3 \cdot 365 \cdot 2.217 = 2\,428 kWh.

Option B. Balanced connection, so equation  applies directly:\theta_p = 10 + 0.70 \cdot (37 - 10) = 28.9 \text{ °C}, \qquad s = \frac{28.9 - 10}{40 - 10} = 0.63

The unit saves 0.63 \cdot 2\,428 = 1\,529 kWh of heat per year.

Option A. Only the cold-water side of the mixer passes the unit, so the flows are unbalanced and the mixing ratio depends on the preheat. Solving the model in the dropdown gives a preheat to 27.2 °C on a cold-side flow of 4.3 L/min, and s = 0.31. The unit saves 0.31 \cdot 2\,428 = 752 kWh of heat per year. Connected for equal flow, the same unit would have saved 37 %.

Electricity and payback. The incremental installed costs are estimates: about 9,000 DKK for option B (unit about 5,700 DKK, plus fitting it into the drain stack and the extra pipe to the water heater), and about 20,000 DKK for option A (unit about 22,400 DKK, minus the 3,000–4,000 DKK of the ordinary channel drain it replaces, plus the cold water connection).

The example shows the three things that decide the result: the effectiveness of the unit, the connection, and the price of the heat that is saved. ## Guiding questions

- Why does a vertical unit usually have a higher effectiveness than a horizontal one of the same length? Why is the horizontal one still often chosen?
- Explain, with the effectiveness of the unit and the flows on each side, why the balanced connection saves the most.
- A family takes baths instead of showers. How much does a drain water heat recovery unit save, and why?
- A low-flow shower head cuts the flow from 12 to 8 L/min. Does the unit then save more or less heat per shower? Does it save a larger or smaller share?
- Does drain water heat recovery pay back faster in a house with an electric water heater or with a heat pump? What about a flat on district heating?
- Repeat the tank sizing worked example in [Domestic hot water](c2-domestic-hot-water.md) with a balanced unit with $\varepsilon = 0.6$ on all three showers. How much smaller can the tank be with night charging?
 

The shower model behind the figures

The model is a steady state shower at flow \dot V and mixed temperature \theta_{mix}, drain water at \theta_d, cold water at \theta_c and a water heater at \theta_h. The unit is a counterflow heat exchanger described by equation 

(4). UA is fitted to the certified effectiveness \varepsilon_8 at 8 L/min and equal flow, UA_8 = C_8\,\varepsilon_8/(1 - \varepsilon_8), and scaled with the drain flow as UA = UA_8\,(\dot V/8)^{0.5}. In all three connections the cold side has the smaller (or equal) flow, so the preheat is \theta_p = \theta_c + \varepsilon\,(\theta_d - \theta_c) with \varepsilon evaluated for that flow.

Connection 3: cold-side flow \dot V, heat needed C(\theta_{mix} - \theta_p).

Connection 2: cold-side flow \dot V_h = \dot V(\theta_{mix} - \theta_c)/(\theta_h - \theta_c), fixed by the mixer; heat needed \rho\,\dot V_h\,c_p(\theta_h - \theta_p).

Connection 1: cold-side flow \dot V_c = \dot V(\theta_h - \theta_{mix})/(\theta_h - \theta_p), which depends on \theta_p. Start with \theta_p = \theta_c and repeat: compute \dot V_c, then \varepsilon, then a new \theta_p, until it no longer changes. Heat needed \rho\,(\dot V - \dot V_c)\,c_p(\theta_h - \theta_c).

The saving fraction is one minus the heat needed with the unit, divided by C(\theta_{mix} - \theta_c). The model keeps UA independent of the cold-side flow, so it slightly flatters the two unbalanced connections: in a real unit, a smaller cold-side flow also gives a lower heat transfer coefficient on that side. The same model in Python can be downloaded here: 

dwhr_model.py.

Drain water heat recovery (

Drain water heat recovery) takes heat from shower water on its way to the sewer. A recirculating shower keeps the water itself. It collects the water from the shower floor, cleans it and sends it back to the shower head. Only a small amount of fresh water is needed to fill the loop and to replace what is lost, so both water and heat stay in the loop.

The example in this chapter is the Orbital Shower from Orbital Systems, Sweden. All data for it come from the manufacturer. No independent measurement of its water or energy use has been published.

Figure 1 shows the principle. The shower starts on fresh water, mixed from the central hot and cold water supply. The water that falls on the shower floor is collected, passed through a filter and a UV lamp, and checked by water quality sensors 20 times a second. If the quality is poor, the water goes to the drain and is replaced by fresh water. An electric heater brings the recirculated water back to the set temperature, and a pump returns it to the shower head.



Figure 1:Principle of a recirculating shower. The order of the components is simplified. 

View script

The data sheet gives a supply of up to 9 L/min on each of the hot and cold inlets, and an electrical power of typically 2.5 kW and at most 3.7 kW on a 16 A circuit. The filter capsule lasts 20,000 L and the UV lamp 8,000 hours. Every night the unit runs a cleaning cycle with 60 s at 72 °C

A weather file holds one year of hourly outdoor conditions for one location: dry-bulb temperature, humidity, direct normal, diffuse and global horizontal radiation, wind speed and direction, and cloud cover. Three abbreviations recur:

TMY, typical meteorological year: the general term for one artificial year assembled from twelve typical months taken from many years of data. It represents average weather, not extremes. The data behind it can be measurements or, as in the Annex 80 files (section D1.4), climate model output.

DRY, design reference year: the Danish national typical year, published by DMI (section D1.3). It is assembled in the same way, but only from months measured at one station and selected with the method of ISO 15927-4, and it is the year used to show compliance with the Danish building regulations. A TMY from another source for the same location therefore differs from the DRY in both the data and the selection method.

Weather files come in many different file formats. The best known is EPW, the EnergyPlus weather file, which is a text format with 8 header lines followed by 8,760 hourly rows. Most building simulation tools read it.

The DRY files can be downloaded as EPW or CSV from 

DMI.

A reference year is one artificial year of hourly weather. It is assembled from twelve real calendar months, each picked from a longer measured record as the most typical month of its kind. Danish Meteorological Institute (DMI) selects the months with the Finkelstein–Schafer method of ISO 15927-4. The method compares the distribution of daily values in each candidate month with the distribution for all years, using temperature, global radiation and humidity as primary parameters and wind and precipitation as secondary ones.

Denmark has two generations of design reference year (DRY), both for the DMI station at Sjælsmark north of Copenhagen, with solar radiation measured at DTU in Lyngby:

DRY 2001–2010, the reference used in building regulations until now.

DRY 2011–2023, the 2025 reference year 

DMI, 2025. Its twelve months come from 2014–2023.

RCP2.6

RCP is Representative Concentration Pathway and reflect future greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere: 

Representative Concentration Pathway

Each RCP scenario was projected for four periods:

2035–2054

2045–2064

2055–2074

2080–2099

DMI considers RCP4.5 the most likely scenario, as it corresponds to about 2.7 °C of global warming by the end of the century 

DMI, 2025.

Extra

Climate models give only daily temperature and precipitation, not the hourly radiation and humidity a simulation needs. So DMI used the projected daily values to choose months from the measured 2014–2023 record: for each calendar month the measured month whose temperature distribution best matches the projection is picked. Where two months match equally well, the one that also matches the projected precipitation best is chosen. Every hour in a future file is therefore real, measured weather from the last decade.

Enthalpy is the annual mean total specific enthalpy of the outdoor air per kg dry air, h = 1.006\,T + x\,(2501 + 1.86\,T) in kJ/kg, with the humidity ratio x found from air temperature, relative humidity and pressure.

Enthalpy expresses the total energy content of the atmosphere (latent and sensible heat). In a building context, it indicates the increased work load on a chiller that needs to both cool the air, as well as shed the water content.

The UTCI column is explained in the section on heat stress indices below.

Take-aways

Four take-aways:

A big step has already happened. Going from the 2001–2010 to the 2011–2023 reference year raises the mean temperature by about 1.5 °C and cuts the hours below 0 °C by more than half, yet 

severe frost still occurs.

Summers get warmer, but slowly. Hours above 26 °C rise from 37 today to 80–90 around mid-century.

Radiation and humidity hardly change. Global radiation stays at about 1,020–1,040 kWh/m² and mean relative humidity at 81–83 %. Solar gains in the future files are those of today.

The projections flatten out. The 2080–2099 file is no warmer than 2055–2074; the two differ only in January, May and October. Because every future month must be a measured month from 2014–2023, the files can never be hotter than the hottest month of that decade.

Air temperature alone does not tell how hot it feels outdoors. Sun, wind and humidity matter as much, and a heat stress index combines them into one number.

The Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI) 

Bröde et al., 2012 is the index used in this chapter. It is the air temperature of a reference environment that gives the same physiological strain as the actual one, for a person walking at 4 km/h. The reference environment has 50 % relative humidity, almost no wind and no radiation beyond that of the air temperature. The inputs are air temperature, humidity, wind speed and mean radiant temperature. Here the mean radiant temperature is that of a person standing in the open, found from the direct and diffuse solar radiation in the weather file (the SolarCal method of ASHRAE 55). The tables count the hours with UTCI above 26 °C, which is where moderate heat stress begins.

UTCI assessment scale

UTCI is an outdoor index. Its ten stress classes

Two alternatives are common:

PET, the Physiological Equivalent Temperature 

Höppe, 1999, is built on the same idea as UTCI and uses the same inputs, but with an indoor reference environment and a simpler body model. Moderate heat stress starts at about 29 °C 

Matzarakis et al., 1999.

WBGT, the wet-bulb globe temperature, is a weighted mean of the natural wet-bulb, globe and air temperatures. It is the index of occupational and sports heat limits. It needs measured wet-bulb and globe temperatures, so from a weather file it can only be estimated 

Australian Bureau of Meteorology, n.d.. :::{admonition} Rules of thumb

- Use the current DRY for energy-frame compliance and for sizing heating.
- Check summer comfort with at least one future file as well, since a 2025 building will meet a 2050 climate.
- A reference year is built from *typical* months. DMI itself says it is not suited for sizing against extreme events such as overheating. Stress-test the design with a heat-wave file (section 5).

Heat waves raise mortality, mainly through cardiovascular and respiratory strain, and the old and the sick are most at risk. The hot summer of 2018 caused about 380 additional deaths in Finland, and the heat-related mortality risk in Helsinki was about 2.5 times that of the surrounding rural areas 

Velashjerdi Farahani et al., 2021.

The summer of 2026 gave similar numbers in western Europe. All three are provisional estimates from the national health agencies. In France, 5,764 more people than expected died during the heat wave of 17 June to 2 July, an excess of 36 % 

Santé publique France, 2026. In England, 2,877 deaths were associated with two hot spells in May and June 

UK Health Security Agency, 2026. In Spain, more than 5,200 deaths were attributed to heat between May and August, the highest number since monitoring began in 2015 

Meteored, 2026.REVIEW: the three 2026 figures above are provisional agency estimates, not journal publications. France (Santé publique France, 22 July 2026) is all-cause excess mortality; England (UKHSA interim report, 30 July 2026) is modelled heat-associated deaths; Spain is the MoMo estimate of Instituto de Salud Carlos III as reported by Meteored, a secondary source. The urban heat island intensity is the air temperature difference \Delta T_\mathrm{UHI} = T_\mathrm{urban} - T_\mathrm{rural}. It is mainly a night-time effect and peaks a few hours before sunrise on calm, clear summer nights. The causes:

Heat storage: brick, concrete and asphalt store solar heat during the day and release it at night.

Low sky view factor: street canyons see little of the cold night sky, so long-wave cooling is reduced.

Little evaporation: sealed surfaces drain rain away instead of evaporating it.

Low wind speed: buildings reduce convective cooling and mixing.

Waste heat: traffic, buildings and air-conditioning condensers.

In Denmark the effect is modest but not negligible. 

Figure 7 shows it for the four largest Danish cities. On the 3 % warmest days of the year, Copenhagen is on average 1.5–2 K warmer than its rural surroundings at night, and on some nights close to 3 K. The difference almost disappears around 09:00. The other three cities stay at about 1 K 

Sørup & others, 2026. In four Finnish cities the mean intensity is 0.5–1.2 K, peaking at about 1.5 K around 05:00 in Helsinki 

Taylor & others, 2025.

For comparison, a model study of 100 European cities at 100 m resolution for 2008–2017 finds an average heat island indicator of 1.43 °C. Green areas and unsealed soil already lower it by 0.45 °C on average, and more of both could lower it by about another 0.5 °C 

Lauwaet et al., 2024.



Figure 7:Urban heat island intensity (°C) over the day in Copenhagen, Odense, Aarhus and Aalborg, for the 3 % warmest days, summer, winter and the 3 % coldest days. Lines are the average and bands the spread, for a machine-learning downscaled temperature product (C4C, blue) and the DANRA reanalysis (orange). Reproduced unchanged from Figure 3 of Sørup et al. 

Sørup & others, 2026, © the authors, licensed under 

CC BY 4.0.Wang et al. (2023), Urban Climate 49, 101531 (Stockholm) is a model sensitivity study and adds little here.

The heat island acts exactly when night ventilation works. 

Figure 8 colours every hour by the temperature difference available for ventilative cooling, \Delta T = T_\mathrm{in} - T_\mathrm{out}, with T_\mathrm{in} = 24 °C. The heat island is set to 2 K at night, the upper end of the Copenhagen averages.

The effect of urban heat islands is more pronounced with future climate, but the magnitude will probably remain the same or even decrease a little as global radiation drops, and mitigating actions are implemented like more green areas in the built environment. Cities are projected to warm by about 1.9 K by 2100 under an intermediate emission scenario 

Zhao et al., 2021, while in Brussels the summer night-time heat island stays at about 3.1–3.2 K up to the 2060s under both RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 

Lauwaet et al., 2016.

New Danish houses are insulated and airtight to keep heat in during winter. In summer the same envelope keeps the solar and internal gains in. Large glazed areas add to the gains, and a warmer future climate with longer heat waves (

D1 Future climate and weather files) makes it worse. Owners report overheating in 11–17 % of Danish homes built after 2000 (Realdania 2024); for detached houses built after 2000 the share is 13.4 % 

Lyhne, 2023. It is not only a summer problem.

On a sunny day in April or September, solar and internal gains can lift the temperature well above comfort levels in a home that hardly needs heating.

A simulation study of new Finnish apartments in timber blocks completed in 2015–2018 found window opening to be the most effective single passive measure 

Sukanen et al., 2023. Daytime or temperature-controlled opening kept the degree-hours above 27 °C within the Finnish limit in most climates, and together with external blinds it met the limit in every climate up to the 2050s. A lower g-value or a fixed overhang alone cut the degree-hours by only 26–36 %.

The solution is not to reduce insulation, as we need it to solve the winter situation, but to apply a sound cooling strategy for the summer situation and the shoulder seasons, where heating and cooling demand alternate within the same 24 h cycle.

To assess overheating in dwellings without mechanical cooling, use the adaptive comfort model of EN 16798-1 

CEN, 2019, shown in 

Figure 1. Occupants who can open windows and change clothing accept higher temperatures after a warm spell.

The upper limit of the operative temperature for category II is\theta_{op,max} = 0.33\,\theta_{rm} + 18.8 + 3

where \theta_{rm} is the running mean outdoor temperature (°C), a weighted mean of the daily mean temperatures of the previous days.

The adaptive limits apply for \theta_{rm} between 10 and 30 °C. Below 10 °C the ordinary limits apply: 21–25.5 °C for category I, 20–26 °C for II and 18–27 °C for III. After a week at 15 °C the limit is 26.8 °C; after a week at 20 °C it is 28.4 °C. Overheating is then reported as the number of occupied hours above the limit in the critical room.



Figure 1:Adaptive comfort limits of the operative temperature for categories I, II and III, drawn from the equations of EN 16798-1. The comfort temperature (dash) is 0.33\,\theta_{rm} + 18.8. Upper and lower limits as shown. Left of \theta_{rm} = 10 °C: the ordinary limits, I 21–25.5, II 20–26 and III 18–27 °C. The points mark the category II upper limit after a week at 15 °C and at 20 °C.

BR18 overheating limits

BR18 limits overheating in dwellings to

100 hours above 27 °C

25 hours above 28 °C

operative temperature in a year. These limits are tailored to the thermal model used for BR18 compliance, with its fixed assumptions on weather, internal gains, occupancy and venting. Use these limits only with that model. Hours from a detailed dynamic simulation, another weather file or measurements in a real house should not be judged against 100 and 25 hours.

Cooling measures should be applied in the order below as it is cost-effective: each step is cheaper and uses less energy than the next, and each one reduces what the next has to handle. It also matches how severe the overheating problem is. The first steps handle an ordinary Danish summer, and the later ones are added as warm spells turn into heat waves.

Reduce solar gains while keeping daylight and view out. Solar-control glazing with a low g-value, sensible window areas and orientations, and fixed or movable external shading that still lets daylight in and gives a view out (

a3-glazing.md, 

D3 Façade design for daylight and low cooling demand). Potentially an overhang could reduce peak solar gains while keeping a view out. Solar-coated glazings are cheap, without maintenance, but the lowest level of the g-value is constrained by the acceptable light transmittance.

Bypass the heat recovery and exploit the deep amplitude of the outdoor temperature in temperate climates. When the outdoor air is cooler than the indoor air, the ventilation unit must bypass the heat recovery. Otherwise a recovery unit with 85–90% efficiency heats the supply air back up with the warm exhaust air, and the heat removal drops to almost nothing. With the bypass open, the airflow can also be boosted, for example at night. It costs only a damper and a control setting.

Ventilative cooling. Large airflows through windows, hatches and skylights, exploiting cross and stack ventilation and night cooling of the thermal mass (

D4 Ventilative cooling, 

D5 Openings for ventilative cooling). Louvred openings (hatches) are particularly beneficial as they can stay open independently of the weather and occupancy. The caveat to avoid is draught when the outdoor temperature is low.

Ceiling fans. Fans let occupants accept a higher temperature. Elevated air speeds of 0.5 m/s give a cooling effect of roughly 2 °C 

Raftery & Douglass-Jaimes, 2020 (

D6 Ceiling fans). The energy they save in air-conditioning typically exceeds their own use by a factor of 10 to 100.

Shutters. In a heat wave, closing external shutters or fully opaque blinds during the day blocks nearly all solar gain. The price is the daylight and the view out, so shutters are kept for the hottest days. Shutters block the airflow through the windows, unless hatches/louvred openings are used as openings instead.

Active cooling. PV covers much of the midday cooling demand, but AC keeps running after sunset: in the 2026 European heat waves the grid strain and price spikes came in the early evening, around 19:00 (

Appendix D: Air-conditioning in Europe, summer 2026). Active cooling also forces the manual/automatic window openings to close.

Steps 1 to 4 are decided early in design, by the architecture, the openings and the ventilation system, and cost little when planned from the start.

In a well-designed Danish house, steps 1 to 5 should be enough to ride out heat waves without active cooling.

The heating demand of the course row house has been reduced to a very low level. The same envelope retains solar gains in summer, and in the 2050 climate the cooling demand becomes the governing design criterion. The façade determines the solar gain and is therefore the first step of the cooling strategy (

D2 Cooling strategy). Solar gain that is not admitted through the façade does not have to be removed by ventilative cooling (

D4 Ventilative cooling) or offset by ceiling fans (

D6 Ceiling fans).

Daylight and solar gain are transmitted through the same glazing, and a smaller window, a lower g-value or a deeper overhang reduces both. BR18 allows daylight to be documented by climate-based simulation to EN 17037 in the form of the metric sDA300. This metric can be used as a constraint when facades are optimized.

The solar gain through a window is\Phi_{sol} = g \, F_{sh} \, A_g \, I_{\perp}

where g is the total solar energy transmittance of the glazing (–), F_{sh} the shading factor of overhangs and fins (–, 1 without shading), A_g the glazed area (m²) and I_{\perp} the solar irradiance on the façade (W/m²). The glazing properties g, U_g and \tau_v are defined in 

a3-glazing.md.

The g-value given in product data applies at normal incidence. It decreases with the angle of incidence, slowly up to about 50° and steeply above 60°, because the reflection at each pane increases. Simulation tools such as IDA ICE account for this; hand calculations with the normal-incidence value overestimate the gain when the sun strikes the glass at a large angle.

records.content:
The fixed shading elements considered are an overhang above the window and side fins at its edges (

Figure 2).



Figure 2:The façade design variables: window size, glazing, overhang and side fins.

An overhang shades according to the profile angle \Omega, which is the solar altitude projected onto the vertical plane perpendicular to the façade:\tan \Omega = \frac{\tan \alpha}{\cos \gamma}

where \alpha is the solar altitude and \gamma the angle between the sun’s azimuth and the façade normal. An overhang of depth d placed at the window head shades a window of height H completely whend \tan \Omega \geq H .

At 55.7 °N the noon altitude is 90° - 55.7° + \delta: 58° at the summer solstice, 34° at the equinoxes and 11° at the winter solstice (

Figure 3a). Towards south the noon sun is high in summer and low in winter, so an overhang blocks the summer sun and admits the winter sun. A 1.0 m overhang over a 1.1 m high, 2.3 m wide south window shades the entire window at noon when \Omega > 47.7°, i.e. from late April to mid-August. The overhang has the same length as the window, so in the morning and afternoon the sun reaches the glass past its ends. The overhang reduces the annual direct radiation on the window from 420 to 162 kWh/m² (−61 %) and the radiation from May to August by 85 % (164 to 24 kWh/m²). From November to February the reduction is 22 % (65 to 51 kWh/m²), which increases the heating demand (

Figure 3b).



Figure 3:(a) Noon sun past a 1.0 m overhang at 55.7 °N. (b) Direct radiation on a 2.3 m wide south window with and without the overhang, Annex 80 Copenhagen TMY 2041–2060. The overhang is as long as the window, so sun from the side passes its ends; diffuse radiation is not reduced.

On east and west façades the irradiance is highest when the sun is low and \gamma is close to zero, so \Omega \approx \alpha is small and an overhang has little effect. Fixed elements block sun at near-normal incidence poorly. Side fins are effective only on narrow windows, as shown below, and movable shading or a lower g-value is normally required. Side fins shade according to the horizontal angle \gamma. Towards south they block the low morning and evening sun, which reaches the glass at grazing incidence; towards north they block the low summer sun from north-east and north-west.

A fin of depth d on each side of a window of width W shades a strip of width d \tan \gamma on the side facing the sun, and the window is fully shaded when d \tan \gamma \geq W. Towards south the effect is small (

Figure 4). For the 2.3 m wide south window, 0.5 m fins on both sides reduce the direct radiation from May to August by 23 % (164 to 125 kWh/m²) and the annual radiation by 19 %, compared with 85 % in summer for the 1.0 m overhang. The fins shade only in the morning and afternoon. Around noon, when the gain is highest, \gamma is small and the fins provide almost no shading.



Figure 4:(a) Sun past 0.5 m side fins on a south window on 21 June (solar time), plan. (b) Direct radiation on the south window with and without the fins, Annex 80 Copenhagen TMY 2041–2060. The fins are taken as infinitely tall; diffuse radiation is not reduced. Compare with the overhang in 

Figure 3.

On east and west façades only the fin on the south side of the window is effective, because the sun is on the north side only early in the morning and late in the evening (

Figure 5). The irradiance on an east façade is highest in the early morning, when the sun is low and \gamma is small. A single 0.5 m fin on a 2.3 m window reduces the direct radiation from May to August by 10 % (east 161 to 145, west 172 to 155 kWh/m²).

The shaded strip d \tan \gamma is a larger fraction of a narrow window. Dividing the 2.3 m window into two 1.15 m windows, each with a fin, keeps the glass area and doubles the shaded fraction. The reduction from May to August increases to 18 % on the east façade (132 kWh/m²) and 17 % on the west façade (142 kWh/m²), and the annual reduction from 15 % to 26 %. Sun at near-normal incidence is still not blocked. Closely spaced vertical louvres apply the same principle, and movable shading also blocks the sun at near-normal incidence.



Figure 5:Side fins on the south side of east (top) and west (bottom) windows. (a, c) The 2.3 m of glass split into two 1.15 m windows with 0.3 m of wall between them, each with a 0.5 m fin; plan with the sun on 21 June (solar time). (b, d) Direct radiation on the glass without fins, with one 2.3 m window and one fin, and with the two windows, Annex 80 Copenhagen TMY 2041–2060. Same assumptions as 

Figure 4.

Fixed shading also obstructs part of the sky and reduces the diffuse daylight throughout the year. When sDA300 is a constraint, this usually limits the overhang depth.

Movable shading (external blinds, screens, shutters) can block more of the sun when required and leave the window unobstructed on overcast days. It requires control, either automatic or by the occupants. This chapter considers fixed elements only; shutters for heat waves belong to a later step of the cooling strategy.

Rules of thumb

Towards south at 55–56 °N, an overhang at the window head with depth d \approx H shades the window completely around noon from late April to mid-August.

Overhangs are effective towards south. Towards east and west, fins are effective only on narrow windows; use movable shading or a lower g-value.

BR18 requires daylight in every habitable room. For unobstructed rooms BR18 accepts a glass area of at least 10 % of the floor area, increased when the light transmittance is below 75%.

However, compliance can be documented by climate-based daylight simulation according to EN 17037: an illuminance of at least 300 lx on at least 50 % of a reference plane 0.85/0.5 m above the floor for at least 50 % of the daylight hours,\mathrm{sDA}_{300,50\%} \geq 50\ \% .

The working plan is 0.85 m in offices, and 0.5 m in residences. The default reflectances are 0.2 for floor, 0.7 for ceiling, all else 0.5.

sDA300 increases with window area and head height, light transmittance and a southern orientation, and decreases with overhangs, fins and external obstructions.

Given the sheer number of design options: different window sizes, glazing types, overhang depths, orientations etc, we use multi-objective optimization.
For instance, given seven window sizes, five glazings, five overhang depths, four fin depths and two orientations, you have 7 × 5 × 5 × 4 × 2 = 1,400 combinations, each requiring an energy and a daylight simulation. A full factorial study of this size is impractical, and most of the runs are far from a useful design, anyway.

The problem is stated as\min_{x} \; \big( Q_C(x),\; Q_H(x) \big) \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathrm{sDA}_{300}(x) \geq 50\ \%

where x is a combination of the design variables, and Q_C and Q_H are the annual cooling and heating demand (kWh/m²) of the zone.

Cooling and heating demand are objectives to be minimised. Daylight is a constraint that must be satisfied.

The two objectives conflict, so there is no single optimal design. A design is Pareto-optimal if no other feasible design is better in one objective without being worse in the other. The Pareto-optimal designs form the Pareto front (

Figure 7). A design that is not on the front can be improved in one objective without a penalty in the other, whereas the choice between designs on the front is a trade-off.

One method is to convert both demands to the electricity use of the actual systems, Q_H/\mathrm{COP} + Q_C/\mathrm{EER}, and select the design on the front with the lowest total.



Figure 7:A Pareto front of cooling against heating demand (concept, not simulation results). Designs with too little daylight lie below the front; they would have lower cooling demand but are not allowed.

The infeasible designs lie below the front: small windows and glazings with low \tau_v give a lower cooling demand but do not meet the daylight constraint.

The optimisation in IDA ICE (AutoMOO in the parametric runs) uses the role assigned to each output, objective or constraint, to direct new runs towards the feasible part of the pareto front. A few hundred runs therefore resolve the front better than the same number distributed over a full grid. The drawback is that trends away from the front are not resolved.

Ventilative cooling or venting (udluftning) means using outdoor air to remove heat from a building whenever the outdoor air is cooler than the indoor air.

It is the third step in the cooling strategy (

D2 Cooling strategy), after reducing the solar gains and bypassing the heat recovery, and before ceiling fans (

D6 Ceiling fans), shutters and active cooling. This chapter deals with the building as a whole: how much air is needed and how wind and buoyancy drive it through the house. The openings themselves, and where the air goes once it is inside, are the subject of 

D5 Openings for ventilative cooling.

Outdoor air that enters a room at temperature T_o and leaves at the room temperature T_i removes heat at the rateP = \rho \, c_p \, q_V \, (T_i - T_o)

where P is the cooling power (W), \rho \approx 1.2 kg/m³ the air density, c_p \approx 1005 J/(kg·K) the specific heat capacity of air and q_V the airflow (m³/s).

In the context of ventilative cooling, the temperature difference is the weak point. On a warm afternoon the outdoor air may be only 2 to 4 K cooler than the room. To remove 1 kW of solar and internal gains from a 30 m² living room (33.3 W/m^2) with a 3 K temperature difference, 

(1) givesq_V = \frac{1000}{1.2 \cdot 1005 \cdot 3} = 0.28 \text{ m}^3\text{/s} = 280 \text{ L/s}

That is about 13 air changes per hour, or 30 times the 9 L/s that the mechanical ventilation supplies to the same room for air quality (0.3 L/s per m²).

Airflows like this are only possible through large openings. They also explain why ventilative cooling works best at night, when the outdoor air is cooler and the temperature difference is larger.

D4.2 Three ways to move the air

records.content:
The air can be moved in three ways:

Natural ventilation: openings only, such as windows, roof windows and venting hatches, driven by wind and stack effect.

Mechanical ventilation: fans only, for example by bypassing the heat recovery unit and boosting the airflow.

Hybrid (mixed-mode) ventilation: a combination of the two. This is the normal solution in Danish dwellings, with mechanical ventilation with heat recovery in winter and openings for cooling in summer.

Ventilative cooling is cheap and uses little or no energy, but it is easy to overestimate. The temperature difference between indoors and outdoors is small exactly when cooling is needed, so large airflows are required. The openings must also actually be open.

The airflow through an opening is driven by the pressure difference across it. For a large opening the flow follows the orifice equationQ = C_d \, A \, \sqrt{\frac{2 \, \Delta p}{\rho}}

where C_d is the discharge coefficient (–), A the free opening area (m²) and \Delta p the pressure difference (Pa).

The discharge coefficient accounts for the contraction of the air jet through the opening. It is about 0.6 to 0.65 for a sharp-edged opening; IDA ICE uses 0.65. Grilles, insect nets and louvres lower it considerably, so always use the free area and the discharge coefficient of the actual product. As an example, the rain-defence louvre tested by Bugenings et al. has a discharge coefficient of 0.29, rated according to EN 13030 

Bugenings et al., 2025.

Because the airflow only grows with the square root of the pressure difference, doubling the driving pressure gives just 40 % more airflow. Doubling the opening area, doubles it.

When air flows through two openings in series, for example in through a window and out through a roof window, the openings can be combined into one effective area (assuming same C_d):\frac{1}{(C_d A)_\text{eff}^2} = \frac{1}{(C_{d,1} A_1)^2} + \frac{1}{(C_{d,2} A_2)^2}

which replaces C_d A in the orifice equation. When both openings have the same discharge coefficient, (C_d A)_\text{eff} = C_d A_\text{eff} with 1/A_\text{eff}^2 = 1/A_1^2 + 1/A_2^2. This form is used in the examples below. If one opening is a louvre or a grille with a lower C_d, use the general form.

The weaker opening dominates. Two openings of 0.5 m² each give an effective area of only 0.35 m², and a large window does not help much if the outlet is small.

The pressure difference has two sources: buoyancy (the stack effect) and wind. Together with the placement of the openings they give the three modes of natural ventilative cooling in 

Figure 1.



Figure 1:The three modes of natural ventilative cooling. (a) Single-sided ventilation through one opening. (b) Cross-ventilation driven by the wind pressure difference between two façades. (c) Stack ventilation between a low inlet and a high outlet, separated by the height h.

Warm indoor air is lighter than cooler outdoor air. The pressure difference between two openings at a height difference h is\Delta p = \rho_o \, g \, h \, \frac{T_i - T_o}{T_i}

where g = 9.81 m/s², \rho_o is the outdoor air density and the temperatures are in kelvin. Air flows in through the lower opening and out through the upper one. Somewhere between them is the neutral pressure plane, where the indoor and outdoor pressures are equal. With two equal openings it sits halfway between them; a larger opening pulls the neutral plane towards itself.

Inserting 

(5) in 

(3) gives the stack-driven airflowQ = C_d \, A_\text{eff} \, \sqrt{2 \, g \, h \, \frac{T_i - T_o}{T_i}}

The stack effect is weak in summer, because the temperature difference is small.

Note

A window and a roof window, each 0.5 m² and 5 m apart in height, with a 3 K temperature difference, give a pressure difference of only 0.3 Pa. The airflow is still useful: Q = 0.65 \cdot 0.35 \cdot 0.99 = 0.23 m³/s, or about 830 W of cooling. Height is what makes the stack effect work, which is why roof windows, skylights and stairwells are so effective.

A single opening also has a stack effect: cool air enters at the bottom of the opening and warm air leaves at the top. The airflow is 

Awbi, n.d.Q = \frac{C_d \, A}{3} \sqrt{g \, H \, \frac{T_i - T_o}{T_i}}

where H is the height of the opening.

Note

A 0.6 m² window that is 1.2 m tall gives only 45 L/s, or 160 W of cooling, at a 3 K temperature difference. Single-sided ventilation is weak, and tall openings are better than wide ones.

Wind creates an overpressure on the windward façade and an underpressure on the leeward façade and the roof. The pressure on a surface isp_w = C_p \, \tfrac{1}{2} \, \rho \, v^2

where v is the wind speed at building height (m/s) and C_p the pressure coefficient (–). C_p is typically positive (+0.4 to +0.8) on the windward façade and negative (−0.2 to −0.5) on the leeward façade and the roof. It depends strongly on the wind direction and on how sheltered the building is by its surroundings. A dense urban site can reduce the wind-driven airflow to a fraction of that on an open site.

For cross-ventilation, the driving pressure is the difference between the two façades:\Delta p = (C_{p,1} - C_{p,2}) \, \tfrac{1}{2} \, \rho \, v^2

Note

With the same two 0.5 m² openings on opposite façades, a wind speed of 3 m/s and a C_p difference of 0.8, the pressure difference is 4.3 Pa. The airflow is 0.62 m³/s, almost three times the stack-driven airflow, and gives 2.2 kW of cooling at a 3 K temperature difference.

Cross-ventilation therefore gives much more airflow than single-sided ventilation, but wind is unreliable. It varies in speed and direction, and the warmest days are often calm.

Design for the stack effect on a calm day, and consider the wind to be a bonus.

records.content:
In reality wind and buoyancy act at the same time. For two openings, the hand calculation follows directly from the equations above, because the two pressure differences add up across the openings:

Stack pressure. Find the height difference h between the openings and calculate \Delta p_\text{stack} with 

(5).

Wind pressure. Look up C_p for the façade or roof surface of each opening and calculate \Delta p_\text{wind} with 

(9).

Assisting or opposing? The stack effect always pushes air in at the bottom and out at the top. If the wind pushes in the same direction (the lower opening has the higher C_p), the pressures add. If not, they work against each other:\Delta p = \Delta p_\text{stack} \pm \Delta p_\text{wind}

Effective area. Combine the openings with 

(4).

Airflow. Insert \Delta p and A_\text{eff} in the orifice equation 

(3).

Cooling. Calculate the cooling power with 

(1).

When the pressures assist each other, step 5 is the same as adding the two airflows in quadrature, Q = \sqrt{Q_\text{stack}^2 + Q_\text{wind}^2}. The combined airflow is therefore always smaller than the sum of the two airflows calculated separately.

Take the house from the stack example: a 0.5 m² window low on the windward façade (C_p = +0.5) and a 0.5 m² roof window 5 m higher on the roof (C_p = -0.3), with a 3 K temperature difference and a wind speed of 3 m/s.

Stack pressure: \Delta p_\text{stack} = 1.2 \cdot 9.81 \cdot 5 \cdot 3/298 = 0.59 Pa.

Wind pressure: \Delta p_\text{wind} = (0.5 - (-0.3)) \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 1.2 \cdot 3^2 = 4.32 Pa.

The windward window is the lower opening, and the roof has suction, so the pressures assist: \Delta p = 0.59 + 4.32 = 4.91 Pa.

Effective area: A_\text{eff} = 0.35 m².

Airflow: Q = 0.65 \cdot 0.35 \cdot \sqrt{2 \cdot 4.91/1.2} = 0.66 m³/s.

Cooling: P = 1.2 \cdot 1005 \cdot 0.66 \cdot 3 \approx 2.4 kW.

At 3 m/s the wind dominates, and the combined airflow is only 7 % higher than with wind alone. On a calm day with 1 m/s wind, \Delta p_\text{wind} falls to 0.48 Pa. The two pressures are then about equal, and the airflow is 0.31 m³/s, or 1.1 kW of cooling.

Now turn the wind around so that the roof window is on the windward side and the low window on the leeward side. The wind then pushes air in at the top and the stack effect pushes it out at the top. The pressures cancel at a wind speed of onlyv = \sqrt{\frac{\Delta p_\text{stack}}{(C_{p,1} - C_{p,2}) \, \tfrac{1}{2} \, \rho}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.59}{0.8 \cdot 0.6}} = 1.1 \text{ m/s}

At that wind speed the airflow almost stops, and the room is not cooled even though both openings are wide open. At higher wind speeds the flow reverses, and the warm air from the room is pushed down through the house. Place inlets low on the façade facing the prevailing summer wind, and outlets high where there is suction: on the roof or on the leeward façade.

Building simulation tools such as IDA ICE solve the same problem as an airflow network, where every opening is a flow element and the pressures are balanced in each zone and every time step. Hand calculations like the one above are still essential for checking whether the simulated airflows have the right order of magnitude.

Figure 2 puts typical numbers on the two driving forces in a Copenhagen summer.



Figure 2:Driving pressure differences from the stack effect 

(5) and wind 

(9) on a summer afternoon (15:00) and night (03:00) in Copenhagen. Temperature differences are to a 26 °C room. Outdoor temperature and wind (10 m) are June–August hourly means from the Annex 80 TMY 2041–2060 file. 

View script

The three modes in 

Figure 1 are compared here with one worked example each, using the equations above.

Worked example.

Now give the room from the previous example a second, identical window on the opposite façade, so that air can flow straight through. The conditions are the same: A = 0.6 m² per window, v = 2 m/s and \Delta T = 5 K. The windward façade has C_p = +0.5 and the leeward façade C_p = -0.3. The windows are at the same height, so the stack effect between them is zero and only the wind drives the flow.

Wind pressure. With 

(9):\Delta p = (0.5 - (-0.3)) \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 1.2 \cdot 2^2 = 1.92 \text{ Pa}

Effective area. The two windows are in series, so with 

(4):A_\text{eff} = \left( \frac{1}{0.6^2} + \frac{1}{0.6^2} \right)^{-1/2} = 0.42 \text{ m}^2

Airflow. With the orifice equation 

(3):Q = 0.65 \cdot 0.42 \cdot \sqrt{\frac{2 \cdot 1.92}{1.2}} = 0.49 \text{ m}^3\text{/s} = 490 \text{ L/s}

Cooling. With 

(1):P = 1.2 \cdot 1005 \cdot 0.49 \cdot 5 \approx 3.0 \text{ kW}

Two lessons follow:

Opening a second window on the opposite façade raises the airflow from about 45 L/s to 490 L/s, more than ten times as much.

The airchange per hour is 24, which in practice will force the occupants to part-close the windows, because air speeds this high cause draught (

D5 Openings for ventilative cooling).

The result is sensitive to the assumptions:

Sheltered site. In a dense urban area the C_p difference may be only 0.3 instead of 0.8. Since the airflow scales with the square root of the pressure difference, it falls to 490 \cdot \sqrt{0.3/0.8} = 300 L/s.

Internal doors. In a dwelling the air must usually pass through an internal door on its way across. An open door of 1.6 m² is a third opening in series and hardly matters: the airflow drops to 480 L/s. A closed door with a 2 cm undercut leaves only about 0.02 m², and the airflow drops to 23 L/s, less than single-sided ventilation through one window. Cross-ventilation only works when the path through the building is open.

Wind speed. The wind speed in the equation is the local wind at the building, not the meteorological wind measured at 10 m height in open terrain. In a built-up area the local wind is often only half the meteorological value or less.

Worked example. A two-storey house has an open stair. On the ground floor a window with a free area of A_1 = 1.0 m² is open, and at the top of the stair a roof window with A_2 = 0.6 m² is open. The height between the centres of the two openings is h = 5.5 m. There is no wind. The house is at 25 °C (298 K) and the outdoor air at 22 °C, so \Delta T = 3 K. What is the airflow and the cooling power, and what happens on the first floor?

Effective area. With 

(4):A_\text{eff} = \left( \frac{1}{1.0^2} + \frac{1}{0.6^2} \right)^{-1/2} = 0.51 \text{ m}^2

Airflow. With 

(6):Q = 0.65 \cdot 0.51 \cdot \sqrt{2 \cdot 9.81 \cdot 5.5 \cdot \frac{3}{298}} = 0.35 \text{ m}^3\text{/s} = 350 \text{ L/s}

Cooling. With 

(1):P = 1.2 \cdot 1005 \cdot 0.35 \cdot 3 \approx 1.3 \text{ kW}

Two lessons learned:

This is five times the single-sided window above, at a smaller temperature difference and with no wind at all.

At night, with the outdoor air at 17 °C (\Delta T = 8 K), the airflow rises to 0.57 m³/s and the cooling power to about 5.5 kW. For the size of the row house this is (38 W/m2).

More openings - Neutral plane

The neutral plane separates positive from negative pressure. With only two openings in series, the same airflow passes both. With multiple openings, the in- and outflow of each depends on the internal pressure and the opening’s distance to the neutral plane, which can only be solved iteratively.

Everything above the plane is at overpressure, so a bedroom window opened on the first floor lets warm air out instead of letting cool air in. The position of the neutral plane moves with opening sizes, so to ventilate the first floor as well, the roof window must be made larger.

The assumed rate is more than four times what one open window delivers. It is only reached with cross or stack ventilation, with the openings actually open and the path through the dwelling open. In the building most openings were balcony doors that could only be secured at a 1 cm opening, or were too windy to leave open. The top-floor flats, with no balcony above to shade them, overheated badly, and solar control films had to be installed afterwards. Openings must be designed so that they can stay open when they are needed: secure, protected from rain, quiet and free of draught (

D5 Openings for ventilative cooling).

This chapter is being reworked and may change substantially.

Bottom-hung (tilt) windows are common in new Danish dwellings. They are suited to airing in winter: the opening is small, secure and protected from rain, and the sash directs the cold inflow upwards. In summer the small opening area and a driving temperature difference of only a few kelvin limit the airflow. Jiang et al. report that bottom-hung windows may not provide sufficient ventilation in the warmer months for this reason 

Jiang et al., 2025.

A side-hung window opens over its full height and, at an opening angle of 60° or more, over its full width. For single-sided ventilation at a small ΔT, the airflow is four to five times that of a tilted sash of the same size. The inflow is slow and drops to the floor, but in summer it is only slightly cooler than the room air and therefore provides cooling rather than draught. The bottom-hung window is thus suited to winter airing and the side-hung window to summer cooling.

This chapter covers the free area of the common opening types, the airflow through them at a small temperature difference, the flow pattern of the inflow, the resulting draught at the feet, and venting hatches. It builds on the orifice and stack equations in 

D4 Ventilative cooling.

D5.5 Flow pattern of the inflow

records.content:
The airflow rate determines the cooling power, while the flow pattern determines whether the inflow is perceived as air movement, as draught at the ankles, or not at all. Heiselberg, Svidt and Nielsen showed in laboratory tests that the flow from an open window can be described by jet theory and stratified-flow theory, and developed simple flow-element models for the velocities in the occupied zone 

Heiselberg et al., 2001.

The balance between buoyancy and momentum in the inflow is measured by the Archimedes number:Ar = \frac{g\,\Delta T\,\sqrt{a_0}}{T\,U_0^2}

where a₀ is the effective inflow area (C_d times the inflow part of A) and U₀ = q₀/a₀ is the inflow velocity. At small Ar the inflow behaves as a jet and keeps its direction; at large Ar it is governed by buoyancy and falls.



Figure 3:Flow patterns from the two window types. (a) A side-hung window opens over the full height; the slow inflow in the lower half drops and spreads along the floor. (b) A bottom-hung window placed high throws the air up to the ceiling, where it attaches as a wall jet. (c) At large ΔT or large flow, the ceiling jet separates at the penetration depth x_s and drops to the floor.

(a) Side-hung window: floor flow. The side-hung window opens over its full height, and the inflow passes slowly through the lower half. It follows from 

(3) that U₀² is proportional to ΔT in purely stack-driven flow, so Ar is about 1 independent of ΔT. The inflow therefore falls towards the floor and spreads in a semi-radial layer in summer as well as in winter; only the temperature and velocity of the layer change. Nielsen et al. measured this for a side-hung window (0.81 × 1.38 m, sill 1.0 m) and found that the maximum velocity near the floor follows the same form as for a displacement diffuser 

Nielsen et al., 2000:u = K_w\,\frac{q_0}{x + x_0}

K_w lies between about 4 and 20 m⁻¹ and depends on Ar’ and the opening area. x₀ is a virtual origin of 0 to −3 m. The maximum velocity occurs at ankle height. In summer the layer is a few kelvin below room temperature and provides cooling. In cold weather the same layer causes draught, and the side-hung window must be restricted or closed. Strong wind adds momentum and can carry the inflow further into the room before it drops.

(b) Bottom-hung window placed high: ceiling jet. A bottom-hung window is normally placed high, as a top light or a hatch. The inward-tilted sash deflects the inflow upwards, where it attaches to the ceiling as a wall jet 

Svidt et al., 2000:u_m = K_a\,U_0\,\frac{\sqrt{a_0}}{x + x_0}, \qquad K_a \approx 7,\; x_0 \approx -2\ \text{m}

The jet entrains warm room air along the ceiling and is mixed and warmed before it reaches the occupied zone. For this reason the high bottom-hung window is suited to winter airing.

(c) Bottom-hung window at large ΔT: separation. A cold jet remains attached to the ceiling only up to a penetration depth x_s, which decreases with increasing Ar. Beyond x_s it separates and falls into the occupied zone. At a large ΔT and a small driving pressure (0.2–0.4 Pa), it drops close to the window and continues along the floor 

Heiselberg, 2006. For a slot at the ceiling of a 3 m high room, model tests show that the cold jet leaves the ceiling before it reaches the end wall once Ar = βghΔT₀/u₀² ≥ 0.02, with h the slot height. In that geometry this is a supply temperature only 0.7 K below the return 

Nielsen, 1990. In cold weather the bottom-hung window must therefore be opened only slightly, so that the jet remains attached to the ceiling.

Worked example. A bedroom is cooled at night through a side-hung window of 0.8 × 1.3 m, fully open (A = 1.04 m², 

Figure 1a). The room is at 25 °C and the outdoor air at 21 °C, so ΔT = 4 K. There is no wind. Is there draught at the feet?

Airflow. With 

(3) and C_d = 0.6:Q = \frac{0.6 \cdot 1.04}{3} \sqrt{\frac{9.81 \cdot 1.3 \cdot 4}{298}} = 0.208 \cdot 0.414 = 0.086 \text{ m}^3\text{/s}

This is 86 L/s and a cooling power of 1.2 \cdot 1005 \cdot 0.086 \cdot 4 = 0.42 kW.

Archimedes number. The inflow passes the lower half of the opening, a_0 = 0.6 \cdot 1.04/2 = 0.31 m², so U_0 = 0.086/0.31 = 0.28 m/s. With 

(4):Ar = \frac{9.81 \cdot 4 \cdot \sqrt{0.31}}{298 \cdot 0.28^2} = 0.97

Ar is of order 1, and the inflow falls to the floor.

Floor velocity. With 

(5), K_w = 5 m⁻¹ and x_0 = 0 (assumed, at the low end of the measured range), the maximum velocity is 0.43 m/s at 1 m from the window and 0.22 m/s at 2 m.

Draught. The floor layer is assumed to have warmed halfway, t_a = 23 °C, with T_u = 40 %. At 1 m, 

(9) gives DR = 57 % and 

(10) gives PPD_{AD} = 22 % for a neutral occupant (TS = 0). At 2 m the values are 23 % and 13 %.

Restricted opening. At an opening angle of 30° the free area is 0.54 m² (

(1)). The airflow and the floor velocity are halved: 45 L/s, 0.22 kW and 0.22 m/s at 1 m, with PPD_{AD} = 13 %.

The fully open window meets the ankle-draught limit from about 1.1 m into the room, which is acceptable for a bed placed away from the window. The ISO 7730 limit is exceeded in both cases, which illustrates the difference between the two models in D5.6.

The floor stream from a low or full-height opening (

Figure 3a) reaches the occupants at ankle height. Whether it is perceived as cooling or as draught depends on its velocity and temperature and on the thermal sensation of the occupant. Two models are in use.

ISO 7730. The draught rate predicts the percentage dissatisfied with draught 

ISO, 2005:DR = (34 - t_a)(v - 0.05)^{0.62}(0.37\,v\,T_u + 3.14)

with t_a the local air temperature (°C), v the mean air speed (m/s) and T_u the turbulence intensity (%). The usual limit is DR < 20 %. The model was developed for people at neutral thermal sensation, with air at 20–26 °C and below 0.5 m/s at the neck. At the feet it is conservative, and it does not apply to occupants who are warm and prefer air movement (

D6 Ceiling fans).

ASHRAE 55 ankle draught. Liu et al. measured the response to air movement at the ankles as a function of the whole-body thermal sensation TS (−3 to +3) 

Liu et al., 2017. The model, adopted in ASHRAE 55, givesPPD_{AD} = 100\,\frac{e^z}{1 + e^z}, \qquad z = -2.58 + 3.05\,v_{ankle} - 1.06\,TS

with v_{ankle} the air speed at 0.1 m. The limit PPD_{AD} < 20 % corresponds to v_{ankle} < 0.39 + 0.35·TS m/s: 0.39 m/s for a neutral occupant and 0.22 m/s for a slightly cool occupant (TS = −0.5). Warm occupants accept higher velocities.

Measurements. Bugenings et al. measured the flow from a full-scale low louvre in a test room at a small temperature difference: the inflow was 24–25 °C and the room 0.4–1.9 K warmer 

Bugenings et al., 2025. The maximum velocity was at 0.1 m above the floor in all cases, also without buoyancy. Calculated from their published data, the ISO 7730 draught rate in the louvre’s path passed 20 % at about 7 air changes per hour (0.31–0.36 m/s), while the ankle model stayed below 20 % in every case.

Fitzner and Finke measured the flow from six tilted bottom-hung windows in a 180 m³ office in winter 

Fitzner & Finke, 2012. In the hour before the velocity measurements, the airflow was 3.3 air changes per hour at a mean temperature difference of 13.8 K, a cooling power of 2.7 kW. With the radiator below the window switched off, the inflow fell to the floor, and the velocity at 0.1 m was 0.21–0.27 m/s with DR of 27–37 %. Hidden until revised (Christian, 2026-10-28)

## D5.7 Venting hatches

A venting hatch is an opening made only for ventilation, usually an insulated panel beside a fixed window. Fixed frameless glazing is cheaper, slimmer and more airtight than an openable window. The hatch provides an opening that can remain open, as it can be made secure against burglary, protected from rain, fitted with an insect screen and attenuated against noise. These requirements were not met in the Nordhavn case ([](d4-ventilative-cooling.md)).

**Escape.** If the hatch is also the escape route from the room, BR18 requires a clear opening at least 0.5 m wide and 0.6 m high, with width plus height at least 1.5 m, a sill no more than 1.2 m above the floor, and opening from the inside without tools.

**Insulation when closed.** A hatch is closed and part of the thermal envelope for most of the year. With gas-filled foam (λ = 0.020 W/m·K), U = 0.12 W/m²K takes about 0.17 m of insulation and U = 0.08 W/m²K about 0.25 m. A panel of that thickness cannot rotate in the opening, so the insulation is divided into two panels, for example a hatch with an inner panel that is fitted in the heating season. Vacuum panels (λ = 0.007 W/m·K) reach U = 0.12 W/m²K with about 60 mm, at roughly 25 times the cost. Built into a prefabricated façade element, a well-detailed hatch reaches U = 0.07 W/m²K with a linear thermal bridge of 0.005 W/m·K.

**Airflow.** For a given area, a tall hatch gives more airflow than a wide one, because the stack-driven flow increases with the opening height to the power 1.5 ({eq}`eq-sh-stack`). The grille, insect screen and damper can reduce the free area to about a third of the hole (34 % for one product), so the free area and discharge coefficient of the product must be used.

**Layouts.** Three solutions are used:

1. a door used for venting and escape;
2. a hatch beside the window, used for both;
3. an escape hatch beside the window, plus an automatic venting hatch high above it.

The third layout is preferable for ventilative cooling. The high automatic hatch is less exposed to noise, rain, insects and intrusion and can therefore remain open at night. Its cold inflow mixes under the ceiling before it reaches the occupied zone, and together with the low escape hatch it provides a large height difference for stack-driven flow.

The room CFD model in [](appendix-room-cfd.md) compares a window and a high hatch in the same room on a cool summer night, with the floor velocity and the draught at the feet for each. The app also includes a balcony door and a low slot.

Under revision

This chapter is being reworked and may change substantially.

A ceiling fan does not lower the air temperature. It raises the air speed around the occupants, which increases their convective and evaporative heat loss (

Figure 1). About 0.5 m/s gives a cooling effect of roughly 2 °C 

Raftery & Douglass-Jaimes, 2020, so a room at 28 °C with the fan running can feel like 26 °C without it. In the cooling strategy (

D2 Cooling strategy), the fan is the step after reducing gains and venting, and before active cooling.



Figure 1:A ceiling fan seen from the side. The jet hits the floor, spreads towards the walls and returns slowly along the walls and ceiling. The air temperature is unchanged; the occupant is cooled by the air movement.

Two consequences follow. A fan only helps when someone is in the room. And it removes no heat from the building, so the gains must still be limited and removed by other means.

The Predicted Mean Vote (PMV) 

ISO, 2005 predicts the mean thermal sensation from −3 (cold) to +3 (hot).

EN 16798-1 

CEN, 2019 uses it to define comfort categories:

Category

PMV range

Typical use

I

−0.2 to +0.2

High expectations

II

−0.5 to +0.5

New buildings and renovations

III

−0.7 to +0.7

Moderate expectations

PMV was fitted to still-air experiments and underestimates the cooling above about 0.2 m/s, mainly because it has no real sweating response. ASHRAE 55 

ASHRAE, 2017 therefore uses the Standard Effective Temperature (SET) from a two-node body model. The cooling effect is the drop in air and radiant temperature that gives the same SET in still air as the room has with the fan running. PMV is then calculated at the lowered temperatures. The cooling effect grows quickly at low air speed and levels off at high speed. ASHRAE 55 caps the average air speed at 0.8 m/s unless occupants control the fan.

SET works like the wind chill in a weather forecast: “it is 0 °C, but with the wind it feels like −6 °C.”

SET does the same job indoors with a model of the body. It converts any combination of air speed, radiation, humidity and clothing into the temperature of a standard still-air room that would put the body in the same state, meaning the same skin temperature and skin wettedness. Skin temperature drives the feeling of warm or cold, and skin wettedness drives the sticky, too-warm discomfort. Two rooms with the same SET therefore feel equally warm, whatever the cause.

The body must lose about 64 W/m² in all three rooms. In the warm, still room A, little heat leaves by convection, so the body sweats and 27% of the skin is wet, which is felt as too warm and sticky. In room B the fan raises convection and evaporation, and the wettedness drops to 16%. Room C is the still-air room that puts the body in the same state as room B. It is found by lowering the air and radiant temperature until the SET matches, which happens at 25.2 °C. The cooling effect of the fan is therefore 28 − 25.2 = 2.8 °C.You do not need to interpret the SET value itself. It is only the yardstick for "same state" when the two model runs, with and without the fan, are compared. The number used in design is the cooling effect in °C.

The cooling effect of elevated air speed may be combined with the adaptive thermal model. In homes without mechanical cooling, occupants adapt by opening windows and changing clothes, and accept higher temperatures than PMV predicts. The adaptive model in EN 16798-1 links the comfort temperature to the running mean outdoor temperature \theta_{rm}:\theta_{c} = 0.33\,\theta_{rm} + 18.8

The category II upper limit is \theta_c + 3 °C. With elevated air speed, the limit may be raised by about 1.2 °C at 0.6 m/s up to about 2.2 °C at 1.2 m/s. Use PMV with SET to quantify a specific air speed, and the adaptive model for overheating assessment of free-running homes.

records.content:
The fan produces an impinging jet (

Figure 1). Below the blades the jet narrows and travels down at often more than 1 m/s. At the floor it stops at a stagnation point under the fan centre and turns sideways. It then spreads radially along the floor, slows down, rises along the walls and returns along the ceiling. The cooling is therefore largest under the fan and fades with distance.

In a 5.5 m × 5.5 m room with a 1.5 m fan, the effect at seated body height has almost gone one fan diameter (1.5 m) from the fan centre 

Raftery & Douglass-Jaimes, 2020.

Larger fans give a deeper spreading zone and a more uniform air speed in the room. Uniformity matters where people sit in fixed places, such as offices and classrooms, and matters little in a bedroom with one occupant in control. Furniture and kitchen cabinets block the spreading flow and leave sheltered zones.

Fan airflow is turbulent and fluctuates as the blades pass. The comfort models in this chapter use only the mean air speed, averaged over time and over ankle, waist and head height (0.1, 0.6 and 1.1 m for a seated person), and ignore the fluctuations. Laboratory studies suggest that fluctuating air feels cooler than steady air at the same mean speed, so using the mean is likely on the safe side.

A datasheet gives the diameter, the speeds, the airflow (usually only at maximum speed) and the electric power. US datasheets give airflow in CFM (1 CFM = 1.699 m³/h), and many EU datasheets in m³/min.

For a given fan, airflow Q, power P and rotational speed n follow the fan laws:\frac{Q_2}{Q_1} = \frac{n_2}{n_1}, \qquad \frac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\frac{n_2}{n_1}\right)^3

Small motors have losses that do not follow the cube law, so the real power at low speed is higher than predicted, especially for AC motors. The efficacy is the airflow per watt:\eta_{fan} = \frac{Q}{P}

It falls as speed increases. The Fanco Breeze AC 132 moves 375 m³/h per W at low speed and 201 m³/h per W at high speed (

The datasheet airflow says nothing about the air speed at the occupant. ASHRAE Standard 216 therefore rates fans by the cooling fan efficiency (CFE):CFE = \frac{\text{cooling effect}}{\text{fan power}} = -\frac{\Delta t_{eq}}{P_f}

where \Delta t_{eq} is the whole-body cooling effect (°C, negative) and P_f the fan power (W).

The effect is largest within about 0.4 D of the centre, drops sharply at the edge of the jet (0.5 D to 1 D) and then falls slowly. Halving the fan speed costs only about 1 °C under the fan but cuts the power far more, so medium speed is often the most efficient. Place the fan within one diameter of where people sit, for example over the bed.
